events.title: Trump says he and tech leaders signed AI agreement that is 'morally binding'
events.summary: Tech leaders gathered at the White House for an AI luncheon hosted by President Donald Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Tesla's Elon Musk are among the tech execs in attendance. Tech leaders and AI researchers have called for a slowdown in development amid rising safety concerns. President Donald Trump on Tuesday said he signed a "morally binding" AI document with tech leaders following a luncheon at the White House , as calls for an AI slowdown reach a fever pitch. Speaker Mike Johnson referred to the agreement as a statement of principles that are "voluntary on behalf of the industry." "It sets forth expectations," he told reporters, adding that the White House will continue to guide industry development. Flanked by major tech leaders, Trump talked up the benefits of data centers and pushed for artificial intelligence self-regulation. "There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation, and we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that," Trump told reporters after the event. "But the self-regulation is very important." He later told reporters he's seeing a "tremendous self-policing." Trump called data centers a "very positive thing" despite mounting backlash over the sprawling multibillion-dollar facilities ahead of the midterm elections. He also told reporters that he officially changed AI to "super intelligence." Tech leaders "want to see communities that are safe and happy, and they're going to make communities very, very happy," he said. "Otherwise, they'll be forced to go overseas or other locations." Outside the White House, Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su said she was "very encouraged" by Tuesday's event and there was "a lot of optimism and a sense of responsibility" in the room. Leaders also discussed some specifics for a framework and industry accountability, she said. "I mean, at the end of the day, it's our responsibility to show the power of the technology as well as ensure that it's very safe," Su told reporters. Concerns over the rapid pace of AI development have intensified in Washington and Silicon Valley as cases of agent-orchestrated attacks mount and major researchers warn of serious consequences for humanity. Frontier lab leaders Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman have joined the calls for a slowdown, facing off against leading tech peers and the president, who previously blasted AI safety fears as a "hoax" and a "scam." Trump said executives want to "do the right thing" for the U.S. following Tuesday's meeting. This week, OpenAI postponed the release of its latest GPT-6.1 Astra model over safety concerns. Just last week, the company said it was conducting an "extensive" review of model behavior. The AI lab has disclosed several incidents of unauthorized model behavior since the infamous Hugging Face attack sparked concerns over rogue AI earlier this summer. A luncheon seating chart posted to Trump's Truth Social account on Tuesday showed the president seated next to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , followed by Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and Google 's Sundar Pichai. Opposite the president sat Vice President JD Vance, between Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Johnson. Other attendees included Microsoft 's Satya Nadella, Anthropic 's Dario Amodei and Tom Brown, OpenAI 's president Greg Brockman and senior administration officials such as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. OpenAI is simultaneously hosting its annual DevDay developer conference in San Francisco. John Ternus, Apple 's new CEO, did not appear on the list. "The main issue that you have and I have is we have to take responsibility for the dangers we're aware of," Palantir CEO Alex Karp told CNBC outside the White House on Tuesday ahead of the event. "All of us do. And by the way, American people don't want separate rules for tech people and for themselves." The luncheon coincided with an all-day event hosted by the president and vice president, where the administration unveiled a new AI-powered chatbot for government websites. Ahead of Tuesday's White House lunch, Anthropic's Amodei attended a private dinner Sunday with the president , following his striking absence from a state dinner for the Chinese president. Sunday's dinner was the first one-on-one gathering between the two leaders, according to a person familiar with the visit. Trump has long maintained that the U.S. needs to maintain its competitive edge on AI. "These are the most brilliant people in the world, and the job they've done is unbelievable," Trump said on Tuesday. "We have a very big lead, and we're going to keep our lead, and it's a very positive thing.

events.title: 'Threshing Day' answers questions 'Fourth Wing' fans have about Rebecca Yarros' series. Here's what you might've missed.
events.summary: "Threshing Day" is the latest book in the "Fourth Wing" universe. Casey Paul/MLB Photos via Getty Images/Red Tower Rebecca Yarros released "Threshing Day" on Tuesday. The book unveils new lore about dragons and their riders from the "Empyrean" series. It also hints at romances developing in future "Fourth Wing" books. Happy Threshing Day! OK, it's not actually Threshing Day, but Tuesday is the day Rebecca Yarros released her new "Fourth Wing" book titled "Threshing Day." No, it's not book four in the "Empyrean" series, which readers have been anxiously awaiting since "Onyx Storm" was released in 2025. It's a collection of the stories of riders from the "Fourth Wing" universe on their Threshing Days, when they bond with their dragons in their first year of training at Basgiath War College. Protagonist Violet Sorrengail doesn't have a story in the collection, as her Threshing Day appeared in "Fourth Wing." Instead, Yarros offers the perspectives of people around Violet, unveiling new lore about the riders and their dragons. The stories have major ramifications for Yarros' beloved romantasy series , including how dragons bond and hints at future romances. Here are some of the most important details you might have missed in "Threshing Day." Multiple points of view The new book includes the story of 13 Threshings, though some of those stories take place on the same day. For instance, Xaden Riorson and Garrick Tavis experience Threshing Day together, and their chapters follow the day from their respective perspectives. Notably, Yarros includes a note at the top of the book that says, "The following text has been faithfully transcribed from Navarrian into the modern language by Colonel Valin Kaori and Lieutenant Ellery Mynna, professors of Dragonkind at Basgiath War College." "Threshing Day" by Rebecca Yarros. Red Tower That note differs from those included at the start of the "Fourth Wing" novels , which are transcribed by the scribe Jesinia Neilwart. Scribes have been revealed to be unreliable narrators throughout the events of the "Empyrean" series, while Dragonkind professors have not, making "Threshing Day" more trustworthy than other books in the series. Yarros confirmed at a book release event in Denver that readers can trust the narration in "Threshing Day," unlike in the rest of her series. "It tells you that yes, this is a faithful first POV," she said. "You guys can trust what happens in this book." How Threshing works Although readers saw Violet bond her dragons, Tairn and Andarna, in "Fourth Wing," much about the actual process remained a mystery. "Threshing Day" broke down how the process works in more detail. First, several of the riders describe feeling a tugging in their chests that leads them to their dragons, as if they are calling to them. Each rider also sheds blood during Threshing. Some scratch themselves on trees or get in a fight before they bond, but in Ridoc Gamlyn's case, blood seemed to appear out of nowhere: "I note a twinge in my knee that, yep, is bleeding. Huh. I must have landed on a twig or something back there." Yarros doesn't explain why each rider bleeds during their Threshing, but dragons frequently refer to bloodlines as sources of power in the "Empyrean" series. Several of the riders also express a need or desire before bonding, which is later fulfilled by  the signet power  they develop. Brennan Sorrengail thinks to himself how important menders are moments before he bonds his dragon and goes on to become a powerful mender. Imogen Cardulo wishes she could take back something she said, and then develops the power to erase memories (more on that later). The correlation suggests that signet powers align with a rider's temperament or desires, though we'll have to see how Yarros explores that concept down the line. Rebel dragons Many of the riders featured in "Threshing Day" are children of rebels who fought against Navarre, whom readers learned in "Iron Flame" and "Onyx Storm" are secretly bonding with dragons that previously bonded with their direct family members. The practice is forbidden in Navarre because it can allow riders to develop multiple signets, creating a power imbalance. In the first chapter of "Threshing Day," Professor Colonel Thadeus Palme reveals that even the staff struggles to tell dragons apart, creating the potential for confusion. There are three novels in the "Empyrean" series to date. Red Tower "I have found that no artist has flawlessly depicted every distinguishing mark of a dragon, which makes telling descendants apart woefully difficult," he wrote. "When in doubt, it is prudent to ask a cadet for the name of their dragon." Because humans rely on riders to trace dragons, the dragons can hide their identities. For instance, Imogen bonds with Glane, who is recorded as being 19 and having never bonded with a rider before her. Yet, Imogen knows that isn't true because she met Glane as a child when she was bonded to her grandmother. Garrick's dragon also indicates he is lying about his identity, though he doesn't reveal who he is. Human lies can also enable dragons to bond with their previous riders' descendants. Xaden bonds with Sgaeyl, and in "Iron Flame," he confesses to Violet that his dragon was previously bonded to his grandfather when she discovers he has a second signet. He didn't answer Violet's questions about how that was possible in "Iron Flame," but in "Threshing Day," Yarros reveals that Xaden's public grandfather isn't his biological grandfather. His grandmother had an affair with his great-uncle, and Xaden's father was born from their affair. The public never knew Xaden's true ancestry, which allowed him to bond with Sgaeyl. Some dragons are also seeking out riders who want to overthrow Navarre and fight venin. On their Threshing Days, Xaden and Imogen tell Bodhi and Sloane Mairi that specific dragons are seeking them out because they want riders sympathetic to the rebel cause, confirming some dragons are playing an active role in the war. Venin clues As any "Fourth Wing" fan knows, "Onyx Storm" ended on a cliffhanger, with Yarros writing that an unnamed rider had joined Xaden as a venin. Garrick and Bodhi are two of the likeliest suspects, and Yarros included hints that they could have turned in "Threshing Day." Garrick repeatedly expresses a willingness to sacrifice himself for the sake of others — particularly Xaden — throughout his chapter, a practice his dragon Chradh questions. Bodhi, on the other hand, reveals that Xaden is his weakness, and he feels responsible for protecting him from abusing his power. Bodhi also worries he doesn't have an identity outside being Xaden's cousin, though bonding with his dragon Cuir seems to calm that fear. Garrick may have turned venin in the hopes of protecting others, and Bodhi could have tried to carve his own path as a venin. events.title: Trump leans on SCOTUS shadow docket more than Biden, Obama and Bush combined
events.summary: President Trump's administration on Monday filed its 41st application to the Supreme Court's shadow docket , a milestone that matches the total number of petitions it filed during his entire first term — in less than two years. Why it matters: The record highlights how often the president has turned to SCOTUS to secure authority to temporarily revive policies blocked by lower courts. What they're saying: "We have never seen an administration run to the Supreme Court with the speed and numbers that we're seeing out of the Trump administration this term," Stephen Spaulding, managing director of the Kohlberg Center at the Brennan Center for Justice, tells Axios. "Keep in mind that the shadow docket, the emergency docket, is used and should be used for actual emergencies," he says. "The administration continues to claim that they're going to face irreparable harm, and that this is an appropriate emergency for the Supreme Court to review, which we think, calls into question how the court's using the shadow docket in the first place." The White House and the Justice Department did not immediately respond to Axios' requests for comment. How it works: The emergency, or shadow, docket lets parties seek expedited Supreme Court intervention before a case completes the ordinary appeals process. The court can, for example, pause a lower court's injunction and allow a policy to take effect while litigation continues. The orders are often issued unsigned and without explanation, complicating how lower court judges apply the orders to future cases. By the numbers: The second Trump administration filed its 41st emergency application Monday. The Biden administration made 19 requests over four years. The Obama and George W. Bush administrations made eight requests over their combined 16 years in office. Obama made three, and Bush made five. Driving the news: The 41st application asked the court to allow the Bureau of Prisons to reimplement a policy cutting off some gender-affirming care for incarcerated transgender people. U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth, a Reagan appointee, ordered the administration last month to continue providing care to people with gender dysphoria while a challenge to one of Trump's 2025 executive orders and a subsequent Bureau of Prisons policy plays out. Zoom in: Spaulding says judges' "primary tool by which they wield power" is to "explain themselves" and why they ruled a certain way. They "explain their rationale, explain their judgment, and what we've seen time and time again on the shadow docket is, in many cases, the court doesn't explain itself, and as such, is not really acting like a court." Spaulding contrasts that with lower court judges who "have taken the time to really consider the briefs. District court judges really are on the front lines of having to evaluate the claims that litigants are bringing." Zoom out: Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson and Elena Kagan have criticized the use of emergency docket applications to circumvent the traditional legal process. Jackson said Thursday during a law school speech that the frequent use of the shadow docket was "having an enormously disruptive and potentially corrosive effect" on the courts. Spaulding tells Axios that consistently using the docket could have "consequences for people's trust and confidence in our democracy" at a time when approval ratings of the Supreme Court are at record lows. events.title: Two Indian nationals charged with smuggling counterfeit Ozempic from China: DOJ
events.summary: Two Indian nationals were charged in Florida federal court with allegedly smuggling counterfeit Ozempic from China, the DOJ said. The scheme purportedly continued even after the FDA seized some of the fake weight-loss drugs in 2023 and warned the public about it. Swapnadip Roy was extradited from Italy and made his initial appearance in U.S. District Court in Tampa, Florida, in the case. Roy is charged with Vicky Ramancha. Two Indian nationals have been charged in federal court in Florida with an alleged conspiracy to smuggle counterfeit Ozempic from China in a scheme that purportedly continued even after the Food and Drug Administration seized some of the fake weight-loss drugs in 2023 and warned the public about it, the Department of Justice said Tuesday. One of the men, 33-year-old Swapnadip Roy, was extradited from Italy and made his initial appearance in U.S. District Court in Tampa, Florida, on Tuesday. Roy and his alleged co-conspirator, Vicky Ramancha, 37, are charged in an indictment with one count of conspiracy to commit smuggling and to defraud the U.S., three counts of smuggling, and two counts of selling counterfeit drugs and holding counterfeit drugs for sale. If convicted, they both face a maximum sentence of 71 years in prison. Trump holds up to $1 billion in bonds tied to institutions he can affect Rep. James Comer expands House investigation into prediction market insider trading Hassett: 'We're still working our way out from' Biden Covid spending Court documents state Roy and Ramancha, starting in July 2023 and continuing to the following April, allegedly obtained counterfeit Ozempic from unauthorized sources in China. The popular drug is made by Novo , which recently rebranded from its name Novo Nordisk. The material they and their co-conspirators allegedly distributed "included counterfeit packaging, package inserts, pen labels, and needles meant to deceive downstream customers into believing they were purchasing authentic Ozempic authorized by the manufacturer," DOJ said. The case comes as the use of so-called GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic for weight loss has become increasingly popular in the U.S. In July, Gallup reported that the percentage of U.S. adults who take GLP-1 medications for weight loss purposes rose to 11% in 2026, compared to 3% in 2024. "And 15% report having used the medicine for weight loss at some point, an increase of nine percentage points" over 2024, Gallup noted. "Counterfeit prescription drugs — especially common ones — threaten the health and safety of every American who depends on the integrity of our pharmaceutical supply," Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the DOJ's Criminal Division said in a statement Tuesday. "These defendants allegedly exploited people's health to pay themselves. We will keep pursuing anyone who seeks to deceive American consumers with counterfeit drugs," Duva said.

events.title: Battery customers feeling 'ripped off' after solar company collapses
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Macarthur Solar customers furious and without batteries after company collapses Murray Wylie paid a $5,000 deposit for a solar battery system that he never received. ( ABC News: Chris Taylor ) A Sydney solar company has collapsed, leaving large numbers of customers furious after they paid hefty deposits for battery systems under a multi-billion-dollar federal government scheme. The ABC previously revealed allegations of rorting and misconduct under the same scheme. Consumer advocates are calling for an urgent increase to protections, oversight and regulation. Murray Wylie was fed up after shelling out a $5,000 deposit for a solar battery system in February, which Macarthur Solar had still not installed by August. The company kept reassuring him, but Mr Wylie had doubts. In late August he drove to Macarthur's south-west Sydney office. But on arrival he was confronted by locked doors and a deserted office. "I was angry because the thoughts that were building up had come true. I wasn't going to get my battery," he said. "You feel like you're being ripped off." When Murray Wylie questioned why the solar battery installation was taking so long Macarthur Solar told him to be patient. ( ABC News: Chris Taylor ) Macarthur Solar's underlying company, Macarthur Energy, had gone bust. Mathew Cox, a local electrician, founded it in 2015. The ABC spoke to eight Macarthur customers who fear they lost large deposits for solar and battery installations that never arrived, ranging from $1,500 to $17,600. Many signed up with Macarthur Solar after being attracted by a generous federal government subsidy, the Cheaper Home Batteries Program (CHBP). The program sparked unprecedented demand, with more than 530,000 batteries installed since July 2025 at an estimated cost of more than $7.2 billion over four years. Macarthur's customers were charged 50 per cent up-front, far above what's considered industry standard. NSW home building laws limit deposits to 10 per cent and leading solar and consumer advocates say the higher deposits may have breached those laws. The state's Building Commission confirmed it was investigating after receiving more than 100 complaints. Macarthur Energy owes almost $3.4 million to more than 79 unsecured creditors, including former customers and suppliers, according to a report by liquidator Daniel Soire of Jones Partners. Sixteen former employees are also seriously out of pocket, owed more than $420,000 for superannuation, annual leave and redundancy payments. Consumer and solar advocates say Macarthur Solar's collapse highlights glaring holes in protections. "The current system is absolutely failing consumers," said Andy Kelly, Choice's director of consumer impact. Mr Wylie had rooftop panels but contacted Macarthur because he was thinking about adding a battery. They came to his house for a consultation. "They seemed fair dinkum," he said. When Mr Wylie checked in at the office about when his installation would happen, he was told to be patient. In June, the company changed the battery he would get. Eventually, he was told it would be installed at the end of August, but that never happened. Mark Barnes is out of pocket $6,500 after signing a contract with Macarthur Solar. ( ABC News: Billy Cooper ) Mark Barnes paid a $6,500 deposit that he fears he will not get back. "We signed a contract in good faith and got nothing," he said. Mr Barnes has now paid another installer for solar panels and a battery system, meaning he has paid twice. The loss means the retiree, who is on a part-pension, has been left with less money to spend on his grandkids. Mr Barnes handed his money over in December. However, he claims the company was repeatedly "stalling". In May, he called the battery system's supplier for help, which prompted a call from the owner, Mathew Cox, and eventually led to a commitment to install the system in July. Despite assurances from the owner of Macarthur Solar that his system would be installed, Mark Barnes says no work has been completed at his property. ( ABC News: Billy Cooper ) That came and went, so he chased Mr Cox, but says he stopped responding. Mr Barnes demanded a refund and lodged a complaint with the New South Wales Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT), the state's small claims tribunal, however the company went into liquidation before his case was finalised. The ABC has seen three NCAT and court orders secured by other customers against Macarthur Energy ordering repayment for amounts between $1,600 and $17,600.

events.title: It's not just Muse: Meta is on an app rampage
events.summary: Jeff Chiu/AP; Meta; Rebecca Zisser/BI Wait, Meta has how many apps now? Photos, vibe coding, and AI assistants: Meta has launched 7 new apps this year. The tech giant is one of many racing to build the AI era's Instagram-scale hit. Meta is on an app rampage that extends far beyond its hit AI personal assistant, Muse . The tech giant has released seven new apps so far in 2026. They range from getting back to Meta's basics of sharing photos to testing AI use cases for everyday people. It's all part of Meta's biggest task at hand right now: Winning the race to build the AI era's Facebook or Instagram. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has also credited AI with helping the company quickly turn new ideas into real products. "AI is helping our teams speed up product development," he told investors during Meta's July earnings call. "I expect it to become a lot easier to ship new apps, so we're planning to build out more ideas and use our recommendation systems to scale them to the people who will find them interesting, as we've done with Threads." In May, Meta globally launched Instants , a Snapchat-like app that it spun out of Instagram. In August, it released Pocket, a vibe-coding social app, and began testing an AI-powered bedtime story app, Storytime, in some regions. Meta also recently shipped three new Facebook apps: Forum (for groups), Seller (for Facebook Marketplace), and Creator Studio (for Facebook content creators). "They're constantly still trying to innovate," Amy Wu Martin, an investor at Menlo Ventures, told Business Insider. This isn't Meta's first time throwing spaghetti at the wall and seeing what sticks. In the 2010s, Facebook had a Creative Labs team that launched a handful of apps. In 2019, the company announced its New Product Experimentation org, which tested, launched, and ultimately shut down several apps, from livestreaming to social apps for music and couples. The NPE org was short-lived, however, and was deprioritized following Meta's major layoffs in late 2022. Now, the company is embracing new products again with open arms. One big reason: the success of Threads. Threads, Meta's bid to compete with X (formerly Twitter), was one of the company's first successful breakout apps added to its roster in recent years. Since its launch in 2023, Meta has touted the social app's growth. In July, Zuckerberg shared that Threads had surpassed 500 million monthly active users, "making it the fastest-growing conversation app ever." The app welcomed advertising at the start of the year, too. Meta's AI advantage While AI has ushered in a wave of new ideas for consumer-facing apps, there haven't been "a lot of winners yet," Martin said. That leaves Meta — with massive resources compared to a scrappy startup — at an advantage. Forrester principal analyst Kate Winick said that, with Muse, Meta is "going back to its roots." The company is "figuring out how to put a very accessible, very friendly consumer-centric wrapper around technology that exists elsewhere," she added. Meta didn't invent the AI personal assistant — startups like Instinct , Town, or Poke have stirred industry buzz — but the company made lots of noise with Muse's rollout. Meta showcased Muse at its Connect conference. Bloomberg/Getty Images The biggest leg up Meta has for Muse, as well as for any app it's pushing, is the billions of users already in its ecosystem. In July, Zuckerberg said that 3.6 billion people use "at least one of our apps each day." When Meta launches an app, it can instantly promote it to its existing users. Have you opened Instagram in the last few weeks? If you have, odds are you've seen an advertisement from Meta suggesting you try out Muse. Meta employed that same strategy to funnel Instagram and, eventually, Facebook users over to Threads . Launching an app into the void no longer cuts it. To stand out in the noise, Meta needs to pour gas on the flame. The company seems to be learning a lesson from its previous app flops by "putting the full might of the company" behind pushing its newest and latest, Winick said. Tempering the super app dream If you download all of Meta's major apps — in addition to the Holy Trinity of Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp — that leaves you with 14 Meta-owned apps. Move all those apps to one iPhone page, and it takes up about half the screen. Instead of consolidating everything into one giant super app , Meta is going for a sprawling approach. When I put all of the Meta's apps on one page on my phone, it took up most of the screen. Screenshot/Meta/Sydney Bradley Dreams of a super app aren't ancient history. Only a few years ago, Meta seemed to be morphing Instagram into a super app with video, photos, livestreaming, shopping, and more. Meanwhile, in China, WeChat dominates as the everything app. Tech executives from X's Elon Musk to Microsoft's Satya Nadella have shared their super app aspirations. "In the Western markets at least, the super app has not been a form factor that has really taken hold," Martin said. "People want to use an app for a specific thing." Meta seems to be giving that a shot. Want to send a disappearing photo to a friend, but not on Instagram DMs? Open Instants. Want to sell a piece of furniture on Marketplace but don't want to deal with the distractions of the Facebook app? Open Seller. This approach could also help Meta as it pushes into subscriptions and looks for potential bundles. "They're really creating an ecosystem" instead of one massive app, Winick said. "And it's persuasive." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Ford CEO says it's 'too late' for Europe to fend off Chinese automakers, but not U.S.
events.summary: Ford CEO Jim Farley said it's "too late" for Europe to fend off an influx of Chinese automakers in the region, but the U.S. still has time to "be considerate" about its decision. Farley's comments come as Ford tries to compete against Chinese automakers in Europe, while also partnering with some Chinese companies on technology and to fill plants. DETROIT — Ford Motor CEO Jim Farley said Tuesday he believes politicians should take lessons learned from Europe when deciding whether to allow Chinese automakers into the U.S., cautioning that it's "too late" for that region but not for the American market. "I think it's just important for us to take our time to be considerate," Farley said at the Automotive News Congress in Detroit. "I watch what's happening in Europe right now, where that was not the case, and it's really something that they have to deal with now, and it's too late." Global market share for Chinese brands jumped nearly 70% from 2020 to 2025, according to market research and consulting firm GlobalData. Chinese automakers' market share in Europe was virtually nothing in 2020 but hit 12% in August, according to Germany-based Dataforce. Farley's comments come as Ford tries to compete against an influx of Chinese automakers entering Europe , while also attempting to partner with some Chinese companies to fill plants and assist in other technologies, such as electric vehicle batteries. Ford and China automaker Geely said in July that Geely planned to build EVs at a Spain plant owned by the Detroit automaker by early next year through a new manufacturing joint venture. "Our answer is pretty simple. We're going to partner with the Chinese where we don't have [intellectual property], where we can be more capital efficient in places like Europe or Southeast Asia," Farley said Tuesday. He also added that Ford plans to also compete against the Chinese, noting that it's preparing to launch its " universal electric vehicle " next year with a pickup truck. The Trump administration sent the automaker a letter earlier this month expressing " profound concern " about its ties to Chinese companies and questioning its strategic trajectory. Ford at the time defended its stance as America's top-producing carmaker and said it employs more hourly workers in the country than any other automaker. Farley's warning also comes on the heels of a high-profile visit last week by Chinese President Xi Jinping with President Donald Trump , who earlier this month said he might be "OK" letting Chinese automakers into the U.S. if they produced vehicles domestically. There also are bills in Congress that could restrict or even permanently ban Chinese automotive brands from entering the U.S. market.

events.title: 10 years on, Geelong and Broadmeadows count the cost of Ford's departure
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Geelong and Broadmeadows economies back on track a decade after Ford closures Anthony Anderson, Tony Travers and Henry Fuller spent many years building Ford vehicles. ( ABC News: Jonathon Kendall ) He worked at Ford for 28 years and still proudly wears a jacket with the big blue logo. He is also one of 17 in his family who worked at Geelong's Ford factory across its 90-year history. For him, the decade since it closed has been difficult. Former Ford workers Tony Travers, Henry Fuller and Anthony Anderson. ( ABC News: Jonathon Kendall ) It's hard to sum up how important the factory was to Geelong. Mr Travers describes the suburb of Norlane as the town that Ford built because it was full of factory workers and their families. During World War II, the plant manufactured long-range fuel tanks for aircraft. When the war ended, it moulded or stamped together large metal sheets into car panels and created the company's well-known straight-six engines. The plant became a microcosm of Australian multiculturalism, drawing postwar migrants to Geelong for the consistent work. Parts for cars including the Falcon, Fairlane and Territory were made in the sprawling Norlane complex and taken to Broadmeadows, where workers welded the panels together, painted the shells and inserted the Geelong-built engines. The final car rolled off the production line at Broadmeadows in 2016. ( Supplied: Ford Australia ) Ford said in its heyday both factories employed about 5,000 people. But that all changed in 2013, when management announced it would close the plants. The American car maker initially announced about 1,200 manufacturing jobs would become redundant at both sites. When the doors closed on October 7, 2016 , many workers had already moved on or been redeployed. The writing had been on the wall for years. In 2013, Ford president Bob Graziano said the company lost more than $600 million over five years on its Australian operations and its costs were "double that of Europe and nearly four times Ford in Asia". Mr Travers was selected to stay on at the factory, working on prototypes, until 2017. When he finished, he found a variety of short-term work, building camper trailers, filling potholes and replacing traffic signs. But he says none of it was as good as his time at Ford. Tony Travers worked at both the Geelong and Broadmeadows factories. ( ABC News: Jonathon Kendall ) "You knew your job every day. When I transitioned to these other places, they did things completely differently and it made it extremely difficult … you had to get your mind out of the Ford way of doing things," he said. Now retired, he remembers the satisfaction of creating such useful products. The closure was such a seismic shift for many of the 600 workers who finished 10 years ago, their bosses gave them a strategy to deal with the disruption to their routine after the closures. "They said on Monday morning just drive into the work car park as per normal, park your car, sit there for a few minutes, and then drive home," Mr Travers said. It touches on a wider feeling among former Ford workers, who talk about being part of a Ford family, in clearly defined jobs. "You're almost institutionalised," says Mr Travers's former colleague, Henry Fuller, who worked at Ford Geelong for 35 years. Henry Fuller has driven buses for most of the past 10 years and is now looking for part-time work. ( ABC News: Jonathon Kendall ) Mr Fuller remembers the years between 2013 and 2016 as tough. In the final days of the Geelong factory, part of Anthony Anderson's job was to help his colleagues find other work. He found the mock interviews the hardest part. "People just hadn't done an interview for, say, 25 years. To get them writing resumes and having the confidence to go and present themselves to a new employer wasn't easy," he said. Anthony Anderson worked at Ford Geelong for 33 years. ( ABC News: Jonathon Kendall ) Mr Anderson agrees many had worked with Ford for so long they felt institutionalised. "When you finish, you will not find the same wages and conditions or the attitude that's on the shop floor here. "You won't necessarily find a comfortable job first off. You may go through four or five jobs," he said. He told many to take time off after the closure, advice he took himself, before he became secretary and treasurer of the Geelong Trades Hall Council. While Ford stopped making cars in Australia, it said it employed about 1,000 people at a research facility in Geelong, testing grounds in the You Yangs, and its Campbellfield site. After the closure, the unemployment rate in Geelong was 6.5 per cent.

events.title: Homeowners are sitting on record equity – and not using it
events.summary: U.S. homeowners have more housing wealth than ever before, thanks to fast-rising home prices over the last several years -- but they aren't spending much of it. In the second quarter of this year, there was a collective $11.5 trillion in so-called "tappable" home equity, according to Cotality, a data technology company. "The borrowers with the most housing wealth are often the least likely to tap it," said Thom Malone, principal economist at Cotality. "They tend to have low mortgage rates, strong cash flow, and little reason to move." A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. U.S. homeowners have more housing wealth than ever before, thanks to fast-rising home prices over the last several years. But they aren't spending very much of it. In the second quarter of this year, there was a collective $11.5 trillion in so-called "tappable" home equity, according to Cotality, a data technology company. That is the amount borrowers could take out in debt while still leaving enough in the home to satisfy lenders. In total equity, borrowers with a mortgage have $17.9 trillion, or, on average, $310,000 per homeowner, which is $6,000 more than they had in the previous three months. While homeowners did originate nearly 20% more second mortgages or home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) compared with the first quarter, it still represented less than 0.1% of the total tappable equity that they could have used. Get Property Play directly to your inbox CNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox. So all that cash sits on the sidelines and continues to compound because home prices in most areas of the country are still seeing small gains. Consumers are also increasingly nervous about the state of the economy and rising interest rates. Taking out a second loan would mean doing so at a much higher rate than they likely have on their primary mortgage, which most people won't do unless absolutely necessary. Mortgage rates dropped to record lows in the first two years of the Covid pandemic, meaning anyone who purchased a home during or before that time has a rate that is at least one third of what rates are today. Those lower monthly payments give them much stronger cash flow in general, so they're able to fund things like renovations or even college tuition without digging into their home equity. All real estate is local, and there are wide variations as equity is heaviest in the West and Northeast. Average homeowner equity levels in Hawaii and California were over $600,000 and over $400,000 in Massachusetts. In Louisiana, Oklahoma, and Iowa, by contrast, equity levels are just over $100,000. Not only are the differences stark but they are actually widening, as home price appreciation is stronger in already high-equity markets. While homeowners in most states have gained equity, some are seeing home values drop and are therefore losing equity. These include states like Texas, Minnesota, Colorado, and Maryland, as well as the District of Columbia. The share of borrowers who owe more on their mortgages than their homes are worth, so-called underwater mortgages, is still quite low at just 2.1%.

events.title: OpenAI agents get rebrand - as 'dots' - while safety worries delay new model
events.summary: Sam Altman has spoken repeatedly in recent weeks about the risks posed by AI agents. OpenAI has chosen to rename new versions of artificial intelligence tools widely known as agents. They are now being called "dots." Company boss Sam Altman, speaking in San Francisco on Tuesday during OpenAI's yearly event for technology developers, referred to "dots" as "remarkably capable, always-on agents that can handle really anything you can think of." OpenAI in recent months has come under intense scrutiny as internal tests of its AI agents have revealed often unexpected and occasionally harmful actions, leading to more public and government fears. Dots, however, were pitched as brightly colored cute cartoons meant to function as digital assistants for people with busy lives. The dots, Altman said, "can handle really anything you can think of." A glossy video was shown during the event, with people speaking to and naming animated versions of their "dots," then giving them various tasks, like building a website and booking afterschool activities for their children. Speaking about "my dot," Altman almost entirely eschewed referring to the tool as an agent, which has been in common use for years. AI agents are essentially AI chatbots that are programmed to operate somewhat autonomously. "You just give your dot a responsibility... and your dots will just get to work and keep working," Altman added. The day prior to OpenAI's Tuesday event, the company said it was delaying the launch of its latest model due to certain safety issues that showed up during internal testing. Since July, the company has been dealing with a series of issues with its AI agents acting improperly. It has faced unprompted hacking into the AI platform Hugging Face, posting to third-party websites images that AI agents took from ChatGPT user chats, and accessing non-public information maintained by the Australian government . OpenAI, as well as rival AI firm Anthropic, previously delayed public release of certain AI models due to potential risks, mostly pertaining to cybersecurity or hacking concerns. Both companies also expect to be listed on the public stock market in the coming months. Anthropic likely will do so this year, while OpenAI is poised for 2027. And both companies have lately been clear that they believe AI poses a genuine risk on a large scale, be it to public infrastructure or public safety. Speaking last week to the UN, Altman pleaded for "national and international" AI standards on measuring the capabilities of an AI tool, assessing related risks, AI safeguards, and the degree to which human oversight over such tools is maintained. Dario Amodei, the head of Anthropic, told the UN that if the speeding development of AI was not properly managed and overseen, future versions of the technology "could be a risk to humanity as a whole." events.title: Trump government ads were funded by Homeland Security, WSJ reports
events.summary: U.S. Customs and Border Protection funded the taxpayer-backed television ads featuring President Donald Trump that have drawn bipartisan scrutiny ahead of the midterm election, The Wall Street Journal reported. Top congressional Democrats say the administration dedicated $20 million to the effort, including funds provided to CBP through Republicans’ “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.” Trump personally pushed for the ads and was involved in their creation, according to the Journal, as lawmakers question whether taxpayer funds were improperly used for political messaging. Taxpayer money from U.S. Customs and Border Protection funded the pro-Trump television ads that have drawn bipartisan scrutiny just weeks before November's midterm election , The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday. President Donald Trump personally pushed for the ads and was involved in creating them, the Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The revelation puts a CBP, part of the Department of Homeland Security, behind a campaign that looks far different from its traditional public messaging. CBP routinely runs ads discouraging illegal immigration. These spots instead feature Trump heavily, tout his tax cuts , attack communism and recycle language from his 2024 campaign. One ad declares that "America will never be a communist country" as images of Trump fill the screen. Another revives his "final battle" message from the 2024 race and attacks the political establishment and news media. The ads have already aired thousands of times nationally and locally. CNBC previously reported that more than $1.2 million had been spent airing two of the spots, according to AdImpact, which tracks political advertising spending. Democrats and at least one Republican senator have questioned whether taxpayer dollars should be used for ads centered so heavily on Trump. Some Democrats in Congress are now calling for investigations into whether money appropriated for border protection is being used to promote the president's political message. "It appears DHS has dedicated $20 million to this outrageous scheme," Sens. Patty Murray , D-Wash., and Chris Murphy , D-Conn., wrote in a letter to DHS on Tuesday, saying the department tapped money provided to CBP through Republicans' " One Big Beautiful Bill Act ." Federal contracting records show CBP awarded $20 million to Maryland-based advertising firm LMD Agency on Sept. 20 for a "National Media Campaign." The one-year contract was fully funded at the time of the award. The award came one day after the Office of Management and Budget approved the release of $20 million to CBP under a "Commemorative Events" funding line. The public contract record does not specify what the "National Media Campaign" entails or establish that LMD worked on the Trump ads. LMD has previously performed advertising work for agencies within the Department of Homeland Security, federal procurement records show. LMD did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on whether its $20 million contract is connected to the ads, whether it is playing a role in the ad campaign or whether additional advertisements or media buys are planned. CBP did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the ads or the procurement contract. Blowback to the ads also spread to federal regulators Tuesday. Watchdog group Public Citizen filed a complaint with the Federal Communications Commission and Federal Trade Commission urging broadcasters to stop airing the ads, while separately asking the Government Accountability Office and Office of Special Counsel last Friday to investigate alleged violations of federal propaganda restrictions and the Hatch Act, which restricts the involvement of federal government employees in political campaigns. The White House defended the campaign Tuesday, calling the spots public service announcements. “These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad,” a White House spokesperson told CNBC. “The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic. We should be proud of our country.”

events.title: Prediction market traders think the U.S. added more jobs in September than economists estimate
events.summary: Traders on prediction market platform Kalshi think there's almost 60% odds that the U.S. added more than 90,000 payrolls in September, and also place a 50-50 chance that it generated more than 100,000 jobs. That's higher than economists surveyed by Dow Jones' consensus estimate for 84,000 jobs made in the month. The September jobs report is set to be delivered by the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday. Prediction market traders are expecting another strong jobs report on Friday. Following August's bigger-than-expected employment report — where the U.S. added 162,000 jobs during the month — traders on prediction market platform Kalshi think there's a 60% chance the country added more than 90,000 jobs during September. Speculators also think there's almost 50-50 odds that the report is once again in six figures. That's higher than the Dow Jones consensus economist consensus forecast of 84,000. On the contracts, traders are asked whether they think the U.S. added more than a certain number of jobs in the month. The market and its contracts are resolved using official data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Traders on Polymarket also think there's about 50-50 odds the September jobs report is in the six figure range. The contracts on Polymarket are resolved the same way as on Kalshi. While the labor market earlier in the summer showed signs of weakness , August's jobs report showed it rebounding. It also gave monetary policymakers at the Federal Reserve greater cover to focus on its inflation mandate, which remains above target , and raise interest rates at its September meeting. The September employment report is set to be delivered on Friday at 8:30 a.m. Before that, ADP's national employment report will be released on Wednesday at 8:15 a.m. ET. events.title: Soho House venue under investigation for food safety
events.summary: Shoreditch House is one of 10 Soho House locations in London A venue of private members club Soho House is being investigated by the local council after a former member of staff raised concerns about rats and out-of-date food allegedly being served. The former staff member told BBC News he was pressured replace labels on prepared food if it was not sold at the end of the day and said he regularly saw rats at the venue. His contract was terminated two months after he first raised concerns, but Soho House said this was unrelated to his complaints. It added that the food incident was isolated and re-labelling unsold food was not company policy, but it did not comment on the rats claim. Hackney Council has confirmed it is investigating food safety and hygiene at Soho House's Shoreditch location. Soho House is a popular haunt for A-list celebrities. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle reportedly had their first date at one of its London venues. The former staff member at Shoreditch House, Kamran Khan, first raised concerns informally about the alleged re-labelling practice before formally filing a complaint with Soho House. Khan was on probation at the venue when he raised the concerns in July, and his employment was terminated earlier in September. Following his formal complaint, the company investigated and told Khan on 24 August there was evidence to support his claim and steps were being taken to address the matter. Khan claimed the practice continued despite the assurances he was allegedly offered, leading him to complain to Hackney Council instead. A spokesperson for the council said: "We have received a report about food safety and hygiene at Shoreditch House and have opened an investigation." Speaking to BBC News, Khan said he was told in a probation meeting to continue the practice. The 30-year-old, who told BBC News he has had several jobs in catering and hospitality said he was told "if I don't change labels on my own initiative, [they] would take that as a performance concern". He said he felt compelled to raise the issue because he saw a lot of children and pregnant women at the restaurant. "I told them that I don't want to be held personally liable for anyone that gets injured," he said. Food served in a restaurant must legally be labelled with information including the best-before or use-by date. Khan also said there had been rats at the venue for a long time and that cleaners were told to check daily for rat droppings. A spokesperson for Soho House apologised for the incident, saying: "This is not how we expect our houses to operate and it is not company policy." They said an external, independent investigation and audit was conducted. "Delivering the highest level of food safety for our members and guests is incredibly important to us," they added. "For clarity, the former employee's contract was terminated for reasons entirely unrelated to food labelling." Soho House membership starts from £291.67 monthly or £204.17 for under-27s. The group opened its first club in London in 1995, and now has 46 Soho Houses in Europe, North America and Asia, as well a string of other up-market hospitality businesses. The company listed on the New York Stock Exchange in 2021, but its share price dropped sharply in the following years as it struggled to make a profit and fought accusations it was losing its exclusivity. It was bought by a consortium of investors last year , with actor Ashton Kutcher joining the company's board. events.title: The Fed's main inflation measure will be released Wednesday. Here's what to expect
events.summary: The Fed's preferred inflation gauge will be released Wednesday and is expected to show little if any change in the year-over-year rate, which is holding well above the central bank's 2% target. Consequently, the readings, which also will include data on consumer spending and income, are unlikely to provide a case against further tightening of monetary policy. Two key Fed officials said Tuesday they still see a likelihood of another rate increase before the end of the year. If anyone at the Federal Reserve is looking for evidence arguing against another interest rate hike, they're unlikely to get it in data due Wednesday that is expected to show ongoing price pressures and consumers who nevertheless continue to spend. The personal consumption expenditures price index, the primary inflation gauge for central bank policymakers, is expected to show increases of 0.3% at both the all-items and core levels, the latter of which excludes food and energy costs, according to the Dow Jones consensus. On an annual basis, the price levels are expected to show increases of 3.7% and 3.3%, respectively, unchanged from July and still well above the Fed's 2% target. In other words, there's little indication that inflation is going to abate anytime soon. "The Fed is going to look at this and say, 'Hey, you know, the core is not moving, and I don't have any expectations or anything to believe that it's going to start going back down in any sort of convincing way,'" said Dan North, senior economist at Allianz Trade. "It's still way above target ... So I think it's really embedded in there to the extent that the Fed is not going to be able to ignore it or explain it away." Fed officials at their September meeting approved a quarter percentage point rate increase and penciled in the likelihood of another by the end of the year. All but two of the 18 Federal Open Market Committee officials who provided forecasts indicated they expect at least one more move in 2026 as they raised their consensus PCE inflation outlook. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at his news conference earlier this month that hiring data along with business investment and private sector earnings show the economy in good shape. "I would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive," Warsh said. Financial conditions are an important input for how the Fed calibrates rate policy. Similarly, Fed Governor Michael Barr said Tuesday that the combination of tariffs and the prolonged war with Iran has meant "we have been knocked off course on our progress toward our 2% goal." Moreover, he added, "I don't yet see a clear trend toward a timely return to 2%." Consequently, Barr reiterated his belief that the Fed likely will need to continue to raise rates, though he did not specify a level. The September move put the central bank's borrowing benchmark in a range of 3.75%-4%. "In my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion," he said. "We want to support sustainable, durable growth in support of maximum employment, and price stability is crucial to that." New York Fed President John Williams noted a third contributor to persistent inflation: the artificial intelligence buildout and the associated demand for related goods. "Fortunately, other indicators are more encouraging regarding the inflation outlook," he said. "Prices for housing services have decelerated, and there is no evidence that the labor market is adding to inflationary pressures." Williams added that the pressure on goods prices from tariffs has largely abated. From a policy perspective, he spoke in more dovish terms than Barr, saying "there is no need for urgency, and we have time to gather more information." However, he did say he expects "one further upward adjustment" of rates may be necessary this year. Wednesday's release adds a wrinkle into the inflation permutations: lower readings in prior months due to revisions the Bureau of Economic Analysis will apply retroactively. Specifically, the BEA is adjusting its methodology back to 2021 for how it measures prices for legal services, software and computer accessories and portfolio management services. The result is that PCE annual inflation readings for July are likely to be revised lower by two or three tenths of a percentage point, possibly taking the 12-month reading down to 3%, according to various Wall Street estimates. That could improve the rearview mirror look without necessarily changing the road ahead as the outlook remains cloudy. Goldman Sachs, for instance, expects that the next couple months of inflation data will be "somewhat less favorable before a more benign trend reasserts itself." Any retreat will come as a relief to consumers who, despite faltering sentiment readings amid the persistent price increases, are continuing to spend.

events.title: ‘The emperor is naked’: Uefa president Ceferin takes new swipe at Infantino
events.summary: Aleksander Ceferin condemns FFE and Balogun affair Tells club chiefs it is ‘time to say enough’ to Fifa The Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, has attacked his embattled Fifa counterpart Gianni Infantino in a scathing takedown of the failed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) project and other recent scandals, saying “the emperor is naked” and declaring “it is time to say ‘enough’”. In a pointed address to the European Football Clubs (EFC) general assembly, Ceferin did not mention Infantino by name but made clear his view that Fifa’s leadership must change. He drew on the event’s location, Copenhagen, to make a comparison to Hans Christian Andersen’s The Emperor’s New Clothes in assessing Infantino’s conduct , making clear reference to the peace prize awarded to Donald Trump and last summer’s Folarin Balogun affair along with the FFE scheme. “An emperor is persuaded that he is wearing magnificent clothes – clothes which, he is told, only the foolish or unfit cannot see,” Ceferin said. “His court goes along with it. Until a child simply says aloud what everyone can see: the emperor is naked. Perhaps the moral of the story is this: convenient words cannot change uncomfortable realities. “Selling part of football’s future does not become development because you call it development. Putting a fait accompli in front of national associations does not become democratisation because you call it democratisation, however big the cheque is. And secrecy does not become consultation because you call it consultation.” Ceferin suggested to the ­hundreds of club representatives present that ­Infantino’s behaviour would not be tolerated at one of their organisations. “Imagine one of your senior executives secretly negotiating away control of your club’s crown jewels,” he said. “You didn’t know. Your board didn’t know. Your players and fans didn’t know. And by the time you find out, the deal is almost done. What would your board do? “Imagine that he creates a peace prize for a political leader, without his own board having any say over its creation or its recipient. Then, that same political leader calls during the biggest competition in the world to complain about a decision on the pitch. The rules say one thing. The phone rings. Then the decision changes. “How many times would this have to happen at your club before the board says: ‘enough’? I think it is time to say ‘enough’. No office, no title and no amount of power gives anyone the right to sell the future of football.” The ongoing war of words between football’s biggest governing bodies had already intensified on Tuesday when Fifa accused Uefa of waging a “misinformation campaign” and trying to influence the race for its presidency, urging a US court to reject Uefa’s request to receive documents for use in a planned criminal complaint against Infantino. Senior figures within Uefa remain adamant that a candidate to oppose Infantino in the Fifa election next March must be found before the 18 November deadline for nominations. The EFC chair, Nasser al-Khelaifi, has been mooted in the past as a future contender but conclusively ruled himself out of the Fifa presidency in the Danish capital. Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football “I have zero interest in Fifa, zero agenda or ambition to be there,” al-Khelaifi said. “I don’t think I’m the right guy for this position. I’m enjoying what I’m doing, having fun. Fifa, not for me.” Al-Khelaifi has designs on expanding the scope of his own organisation. In his speech to the general assembly he said “now is the time to create World Football Clubs”, explicitly stating that a representative body including those beyond Europe should be formed. “We are more than proud and happy if we can help and contribute outside of Europe for our colleagues from different clubs in the world,” he said later.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters SPONSORED POST: How agentic AI, real-time visibility, and stronger governance can help enterprises protect critical services and manage increasingly complex IT environments. When a critical application fails, the last thing an IT team needs is a debate over who's responsible. Yet in complex enterprise environments, network, application, and compute teams often rely on separate legacy monitoring tools, each providing only part of the picture. Identifying the root cause can become a time-consuming exercise while essential services remain unavailable. As organizations expand their use of AI, hybrid infrastructure, and sovereign cloud environments, the challenge is becoming more pressing. The systems supporting critical services are growing more interconnected, while the need for resilience, operational efficiency, and effective governance continues to increase. AI agents are starting to take on some of that operational load, but an agent reasoning from legacy monitoring data sees the same partial picture the humans do. But are enterprise leaders seeing the same risks as the teams responsible for keeping these systems running? Research by Virtana suggests a significant observability gap between what boardrooms believe they know about their IT environments and what frontline operators experience. In this interview, The Register's Tim Phillips speaks with Paul Appleby, CEO of Virtana, about the limitations of legacy monitoring approaches and how agentic observability could help organizations gain a clearer picture of their infrastructure. Appleby explores why fragmented legacy monitoring can leave IT teams struggling to distinguish the cause of an incident from its symptoms, and how agentic observability, which correlates real-time telemetry across applications, cloud, infrastructure, networks, and AI systems, gives AI agents the context to accelerate root cause analysis and remediation. The discussion also examines the growing importance of observability for data sovereignty and AI infrastructure. As enterprises invest in AI factories and increasingly complex workloads, Appleby considers how organizations can maintain visibility across the technology stack, strengthen governance, and address operational risks before they disrupt critical services. For IT leaders, the interview offers a perspective on moving beyond the traditional focus on proving which team wasn't responsible, toward faster resolution, preventative observability, and more resilient operations. It also raises an important question for executive teams: Is investment in governance and operational controls keeping pace with the infrastructure and AI services their businesses increasingly depend on? events.title: OpenAI hit with landmark lawsuit following Hugging Face hack
events.summary: A public interest law group hit OpenAI with a lawsuit Tuesday over its breach of tech company Hugging Face , seeking court-ordered restrictions to prevent future hacks. The big picture: The rogue hacking incident — and reports of tens of thousands of other possible examples of problematic agentic behavior — demonstrated the urgent risk of AI agents escaping their testing environments, bypassing guardrails and outpacing their creators . The case tests an increasingly urgent question as AI agents gain power: Who bears legal responsibility when an agent blows past its guardrails and causes real-world harm? Driving the news: " OpenAI is responsible for the conduct of its agents," Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology (LASST), representing itself alongside Gerstein Harrow LLP, argued in its suit filed in California Superior Court Tuesday. They allege OpenAI agents "knowingly" accessed Hugging Face without permission and that employees or officers caused that access "either with actual knowledge or in willful blindness." The suit aims to block development practices that allow AI agents to autonomously cause outside harm, LASST founder Tyler Whitmer tells Axios and ensures there are "legal mechanisms that tie these harms back to a responsible human" or corporate actor when an AI agent causes harm. Whitmer hopes an injunction would "incentivize OpenAI and … the industry to alter their development processes in a way that would prevent this from happening" again. Zoom in: The organization sued under California's Unfair Competition Law , arguing OpenAI's "unlawful and unfair business practices" diverted work and resources to responding to the Hugging Face incident. It also argued "OpenAI's insistence on externalizing the harms of its unsafe decision-making is a fundamentally unfair business practice," nodding to a letter from OpenAI and other tech leaders calling on organizations to "[m]ake cyber defense an immediate leadership priority." The suit also argued OpenAI violated California's data access and fraud statutes as a result of its decision to disable cyber guardrails for its agents and deploy them on tasks they couldn't solve as intended, among other practices. LASST is asking for an injunction barring OpenAI from "knowingly accessing or causing to be accessed" computers without authorization and from "engaging in unlawful or unfair business practices" or "knowingly employing an unfair business practice that threatens serious harm on the public." The intrigue: California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) signed a law last year that prevents defendants from escaping liability by arguing the AI acted on its own. Tuesday's suit marks another court challenge for the ChatGPT maker, which Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier (R) asked a court Monday to prevent OpenAI from further developing its tech for now. What we're watching: The suit also comes as a cast of AI leaders and power players — including OpenAI President Greg Brockman — are set to meet with President Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson on Tuesday as calls for federal intervention mount. But OpenAI is trying to walk a fine line, Axios' Maria Curi and Ina Fried report : On the other coast, in San Francisco, CEO Sam Altman is at a conference touting the new science coming out of its labs. events.title: Pilots, aircrew face higher radiation-related cancer death rates, study finds
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Radiation-related cancer deaths more common in aircrew than other occupations, study finds The US study found 6.9 per cent of deaths among flight attendants were caused by radiation-related cancers. ( Getty Images: James Lauritz ) A new study found almost 7 per cent of all deaths among US flight attendants and pilots from 2020-2024 were due to radiation-related cancer, the highest rate among the 500 occupations studied. The researchers suggested increased mortality could be caused by cosmic radiation, which aircrews are exposed to at higher levels. The Transport Workers' Union and experts have called for better protections for workers but the Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency says the results are not clear cut. A large US study has found that of 500 occupations, flight attendants and pilots had the highest proportion of radiation-related cancer deaths. The study, published in JAMA Internal Medicine , looked at almost 13 million US death records from 2020–2024. The researchers found that radiation-related cancers (such as leukaemia, breast, thyroid and skin cancers) were listed on 6.9 per cent of deaths among flight attendants and 6.7 per cent of deaths among pilots. This was the highest and second-highest proportions of radiation-related cancer deaths across all occupation groups in the US. In comparison, ground crews, which work in a similar environment to aircrew but without the air travel, did not have the same elevated proportion of radiation-related cancer deaths as the pilots and flight attendants. "These findings support consideration of occupational radiation protections for aircrew members commensurate with their exposure level," the researchers concluded. While the research was based on US data, it might be applicable to air crews around the world, said Catherine Olsen, an epidemiologist and melanoma researcher at QIMR Berghofer who was not involved with the study. Flight crews spend much longer in the air than the average frequent flyer, and are more exposed to cosmic radiation — high energy particles from the Sun and other cosmic sources. Exposure to too much cosmic radiation can damage our DNA, cause radiation sickness and increase the risk of some cancers. On the ground, we are well protected from cosmic radiation. Australians on average receive 3.4 millisieverts a year from all types of ionising radiation. But the thinner atmosphere at higher elevations where airplanes fly lets more radiation sneak through. Nuclear workers had lower rates of radiation-related cancers than aircrews. ( Getty Images: skynesher ) Aircrews are among the most exposed groups of workers to ionising radiation, according to the Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency (ARPANSA). It limits aircrew exposure to 20 millisieverts (mSv) per year averaged over five years — about the same as three chest CT scans. The organisation also has a lower "reference level" of 6 mSv per year, that they recommend aircrew and airlines try to maintain. While it is well known that aircrews are exposed to increased cosmic radiation, linking that to increased cancer mortality is complicated. Dr Olsen said that comparing air crews with other occupations like ground crews and nuclear workers provided more evidence that the cosmic radiation could be causing the increase in radiation-related cancer deaths. "I'm confident that it's a very well conducted study," she said. "A limitation is that there's a possibility that there might be misclassification on death certificates if that occupation is not recorded properly." But an ARPANSA spokesperson said the study did not account for lifestyle factors like alcohol consumption, circadian rhythm disruption and lack of sun protection, which can also increase the risk of radiation-related cancers. Dr Olsen said if there was an increase risk of death in these occupations, airlines and health care professionals needed to be more aware. "When those flight crew and pilots are having their medical checks, there should be a heightened kind of degree of concern of any symptoms that might be related to cancer." Ebanie Fletcher, who has worked as an Australian flight attendant for more than 20 years, said radiation risk was not something that was discussed by the airlines. "None of it is really talked about, especially not by our safety regulators or the industry as a whole," she said. events.title: AMD's 192 GB Gorgon Halo prices might leave you petrified
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Regular pricing starts at $6,799 - all that memory doesn't come cheap Zuckerberg touts enterprise AI push because Meta would never do anything to damage your reputation now Schneider gives datacenter switchgear the software-defined treatment 4 hours ago Investors are pricing in a 32.6% AI productivity boost for software engineers 7 hours ago AMD bets $8.2B that worlds matter more than words in AI 21 hours ago AWS needs to embrace its place as the Home Depot of AI infrastructure 22 hours ago The first systems powered by AMD's Gorgon Halo system-on-chip (SoC) platform have arrived, boasting up to 192 GB of unified memory on board. That's enough to put DeepSeek V4 Flash on your desk if you can afford to pay a hefty premium for all that RAM. GMKtec's EVO-X5 Pro is among the first to feature the House of Zen's top-specced Ryzen AI Max+ 495 SoC — you can see why we're just going to call it Gorgon Halo from here on out — but with regular pricing starting at $6,799, all that memory doesn't come cheap. But for local AI enthusiasts and perhaps privacy-conscious small businesses, it might be worth it just to run larger, more capable models from the security of their homes and offices. At 4-bit precision, Gorgon Halo is equipped with enough memory to run models to around 345 billion parameters on Linux or 320 billion parameters on Windows. The difference here comes down to memory partitioning. On Windows, you'll need to allocate 160 GB of memory to the GPU, while the Linux kernel and AMD's GPU drivers enable users to take advantage of nearly all of the available memory. This puts high-profile frontier models like the 284 billion parameter DeepSeek V4 Flash or Z.AI's 320 billion parameter GLM-5.3-Flash within reach of Gorgon Halo customers. Announced earlier this year , Gorgon Halo is essentially a factory overclocked version of the Strix Halo APU that powers AMD's AI Halo workstation that we reviewed this summer. Both chips can be had with up to 16 Zen 5 cores, a 40-compute-unit integrated GPU, and an XDNA 2-based NPU to power all the Copilot+ features you didn't ask for but Microsoft is pushing on you anyway. The big difference between the chips is that AMD has bumped up the clocks by about 100 MHz across the board, and Gorgon Halo now supports 192 GB of faster 8,533 MT/s LPDDR5x memory compared to Strix Halo's 128 GB of 8,000 MT/s. In terms of performance, we don't expect the clock bump to make a meaningful difference. With that said, the faster memory could help a little bit for local AI enthusiasts. Large language model (LLM) inference — that is, the process of running pre-trained models — is predominantly memory bound. That means the faster your memory is, the faster the system can generate tokens. But while Gorgon Halo does achieve high memory bandwidth at 273 GB/s, that's only about 6.5 percent faster than Strix Halo at 256 GB/s. At most, you can expect to see a few more tokens a second on highly optimized models. Gorgon's main attraction is really the prospect of higher memory capacity. But as we mentioned before, the ongoing memory shortage has not been kind to consumer electronics. A year ago, a 128 GB Strix Halo box would have set you back between $2,000 and $3,000 depending on OEM. DDR5 prices have skyrocketed since then and by the time AMD launched its AI Halo workstation this summer, prices had jumped to $4,000. With 50 percent more memory, you can expect Gorgon Halo-based products to be even pricier. The GMKtec unit is already 64 percent more expensive and the brand is usually on the more affordable side of things. More premium brands like Framework and notebooks like HP's ZBook Ultra G3a will likely command a steep premium. Unfortunately for AMD, there's not a lot that can be done. LPDDR5x is in short supply thanks to the AI boom. Each NVL72 rack Nvidia sells is packed with between 36 and 54 TB of the stuff, and that's just CPU memory. The situation is only going to get worse as AMD embraces LPDDR5x for its own AI-optimized Verano Epycs .
