REGISTER HERE. Wabi , the AI startup that allowed anyone to use prompts to build apps , is undergoing a slight pivot as demand for AI agents, like Meta’s Muse and Instinct , takes off. The company announced this week that Wabi is now becoming an AI messenger of sorts — but one that’s still capable of making apps to help you get things done. The startup’s founder Eugenia Kuyda, who previously founded the AI companion startup Replika, described Wabi 2.0, as the new experience is called, as a “personal agent that does stuff for you and builds the interface you need in the moment.” Introducing Wabi 2.0: a new kind of messenger that makes apps and gets things done for you and your friends. We’re building the OS for the agentic era – software that adapts to your life, gets things done, and makes more room for the people and things that matter. Invite-only… pic.twitter.com/x9UlzrJSXs — wabi (@wabi) September 28, 2026 It’s a similar value proposition to that offered by the original version of Wabi — but one that users will interact with in a different way. Instead of positioning itself up against other vibe-coding tools, Wabi 2.0 aims to compete more directly with AI agents that combine both conversations and productivity tasks in a single interface. It also comes as companies like OpenAI and others are thinking about how apps will work inside their more generalized chatbot user interfaces; for instance, OpenAI today announced at its Dev Day an update to ChatGPT’s plugins, which will allow apps to offer interactive experiences within ChatGPT, and where the app’s name gets pinned in a more visible spot on ChatGPT’s sidebar. In a post on X , Kudya explained how Wabi’s new experience will make more sense for consumers, who want to do more than just type to an agent. “The more you use a chat-only agent, the worse the experience gets. Your history and ongoing tasks end up buried in one endless scroll. People don’t just want to type-type-type; They want to tap-tap-tap, scroll, and look. They love what agents can do, but they also like software,” she wrote. “The most powerful agent will be the one that combines both.” The idea is that as a user asks the agent to perform a task, it could create a user interface on demand to help complete whatever the request may be. For instance, Kudya suggested users could build things like a calorie tracker, a weightlifting log, and a weight tracker, which would be accessible in her thread about health-related topics. In another thread focused on family, users could create a calendar of the kids’ activities, a language learning app, an app that keeps up with local kid-friendly events, and other things that relate to parenting, household management, or the kids’ interests. “So far, personal agents have been one person, one chat, a stream of one-off tasks. events.title: A woman in her 30s noticed her period was irregular. It turns out, she had ovarian cancer.
events.summary: Natalie May was diagnosed with stage 1 ovarian cancer at 37 years old. Courtesy of Natalie May A woman was diagnosed with early ovarian cancer after she had an irregular menstrual period. She was 37, more than a decade younger than typical patients, and a rare case of stage 1. Ovarian cancers are on the rise in younger people and are typically missed due to subtle symptoms. In front of a crowd of about a thousand people, Natalie May stepped onstage to talk about something she'd barely even spoken to close friends about — her vagina. Her husband was mortified. But by 2018, May had gotten used to being known as "the vagina lady" to audiences ranging from 12 to 200, sharing her own experience to help others recognize the early warning signs of ovarian cancer . "It's not just something that happens to someone else. It can happen to us," she told Business Insider. May, who lives in Adelaide, Australia, was 37 years old when she was diagnosed with stage 1 ovarian cancer. Now in her 50s and one of Australia's leading papercraft experts, May uses her scrapbooking classes and workshops to raise awareness that cancer can often develop for months if symptoms go unnoticed. Cancer has become a growing concern for younger people, as more patients in their 20s and 30s are diagnosed with ovarian cancer, colon cancer , and breast cancer. "There are so many different things put down to 'just being a woman.' That's bullshit," May said. "You really need to know what's normal for your own body." Subtle signs of ovarian cancer Around 2013, May noticed bright red spotting that escalated to full bleeding, which was unusual because she had recently finished her normal menstrual cycle . "It was out of the blue," May said. "Within two days, I was going through a pad an hour." She booked an appointment with her primary care doctor, who referred her for follow-up scans after initial testing revealed she had lost a lot of blood. May was so confident that the follow-up appointment would be mundane, she brought her husband and daughter, 10 years old at the time, along with her. She had no family history of cancer, and a diagnosis never crossed her mind. Then the doctor came in to discuss the results. When the nurse first took her daughter out of the room, May knew something was seriously wrong. Australian papercrafter Natalie May was diagnosed with ovarian cancer in her 30s. She's since used her artistic platform to raise awareness. Courtesy of Natalie May Imaging had found a six-centimeter cyst on her left ovary, which they suspected was cancerous. The initial diagnosis felt like "a complete and total blur" of panic and shock, she recalled. Leading up to the diagnosis, May said she had felt she was in the best shape of her life, working with a personal trainer and exercising regularly. She had been losing weight: in retrospect, an early symptom of cancer . With no other common signs of ovarian cancer , like bloating or abdominal pain, it would have been easy to ignore. May said trusting her gut and seeking help likely saved her life. In the two weeks between the initial scan and her first surgery, the mass on her ovary had developed aggressively, nearly doubling in size. "By listening to my body and acting straightaway rather than just pushing it aside, I prevented it from turning into stage two, three, or even four," May said. Early treatment is key to surviving ovarian cancer May didn't know much about ovarian cancer . She had to Google it when she got home from the doctor's appointment. She learned that stage 1 diagnoses are rare because the cancer often spreads before patients seek help. While May said she was lucky to have an early diagnosis , her treatment plan was far from simple. She underwent an initial surgery to remove the cyst, followed by a radical hysterectomy. Recovery involved two weeks in the hospital, unable to sit up or do much else, and the healing process was delayed by months of chemotherapy to help reduce the risk of any lingering cancer cells. Cancer treatment was a difficult ordeal, with symptoms like hair loss. May said she experienced depression and anxiety for months after she was in remission. Courtesy of Natalie May Ovarian cancer is highly prone to coming back after remission; some studies estimate that up to 70% of patients experience recurrence on average, and it's more likely to increase with later-stage cancers. "It took probably four months for me to be able to walk, to drive unassisted, to get back to living," May said. "All of a sudden, I had to go completely dark and cancel a heap of jobs and stop what I was doing to go through all of this treatment." Cancer is on the rise in younger people For six months, May went to her chemotherapy appointment every Friday. It was there she first realized she was an outlier — more than a decade younger than the typical ovarian cancer patient in their early 60s. "The only time I realized I was quite young was when I was sitting in the chemo ward, and I was the youngest person in the room," May added. That was in 2013. Over the past decade, early-onset cases of multiple types of cancer have been increasingly common in the US. May said advocacy has helped her work through the lasting mental health toll of her diagnosis, which led to anxiety and depression in the years after her treatment. At her crafting workshops — predominantly attended by women — she takes comfort in being open and blunt about her cancer experience, urging women of all ages to know the signs. "As women, we tend to put everybody else before ourselves, and we ignore symptoms," May said. "The thing we forget is that we can't look after other people unless we look after ourselves first." events.title: What smart people are saying about Anthropic's leaked IPO prospectus numbers
events.summary: Anthropic's reported IPO prospectus has some truly eye-watering numbers. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images Anthropic's IPO prospectus is out, and the numbers are astonishing. For example, it spent $7.3 billion on computing and faces $518 billion in fresh commitments. Business Insider put together a list of what smart people are saying about those numbers. Anthropic's IPO math is staggering. The AI lab generated nearly $4.6 billion in revenue last year — about 12 times its 2024 total — while recording a $42 billion net loss, per an IPO prospectus seen by Reuters . The company spent $7.33 billion on compute and infrastructure in 2025 and has $518 billion in future cloud, computing, and infrastructure obligations. The prospectus could value the company at $2 trillion, while the company is predicting an IPO after the November midterm elections, Reuters reported. The report comes as Anthropic has been on a bit of a roller coaster ride. Employees, including CEO Dario Amodei, have warned that AI labs haven't secured a firm grasp on their autonomous AI systems amid reports of security breaches and hacking incidents. Anthropic dedicated 80 of the IPO's 261 pages to risk factors, per the Financial Times . Meanwhile, last week, Anthropic released Claude Opus 5.5, its latest flagship model. Here is what some smart techies and market watchers have said about the gobsmacking numbers. The company didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Lale Akoner, global market strategist at eToro Akoner told Business Insider that the prospectus shows that Anthropic has a lot of work to do. While the 2025 revenue growth shows how fast demand has accelerated, the "more meaningful figure is the $8.1 billion operating loss," she said, because the company is a "long way from proving it can turn rapid revenue growth into sustainable profits." Still, if the IPO is successful, the effects could ripple through the market, Akoner said. She said it could set the stage for OpenAI's expected IPO and attract investment away from other tech companies. "Ultimately, investors will need to decide whether Anthropic's growth can justify both its enormous valuation and its future spending commitments," she said. Gary Marcus, professor emeritus of psychology at NYU Marcus, a consistent AI skeptic, sees a perverse incentive. "Anthropic's proposed valuation is easily calculated, as -50 times 2025 losses," he wrote on X. "The more they lose, the more they win!" His post gets at the unease behind the huge numbers: Wall Street may reward companies for growth and infrastructure spending, well before they prove their businesses can generate consistent profits. He also said that investors have to paper over concerns about rogue AI agents. "You can only get there by largely ignoring all the ways things would go wrong," he wrote . "If I tell you that there is a 10% chance of annihilating humanity, the expected value is a loss of 800 million people, which would be by far the worst disaster in human history." Ross Hendricks, an equity analyst at Porter & Company Hendricks sees a bill hiding in Anthropic's fine print. About $34 billion of the company's 2025 loss was a noncash accounting charge — meaning that amount did not leave the company's bank account last year. Instead, he said, the company could issue more shares, meaning early investors own a smaller slice of the company. "The shareholder dilution on this will be something to behold," Hendricks wrote . Jake Williams, cybersecurity risk expert In a post on Bluesky , Williams zeroed in on another disclosure: nearly a quarter of Anthropic's 2025 revenue came from two customers. "Siri, is it good when huge chunks of my revenue come from only two companies?" he wrote. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Oura pulls $15bn stock market listing days after announcement
events.summary: Oura's chief executive Tom Hale wears one of the company's smart rings Oura has pulled its plan to sell shares in its business on the US stock market, in a move which would have valued the firm at $15bn (£11.3bn), just days after announcing it. The maker of smart rings which track their owners' health said it would postpone its flotation "due to uncertainty in the Initial Public Offering (IPO) market" and did not say when it might go ahead. Oura had filed official documents setting out plans to raise up to $2.2bn by offering shares in the business to investors just over a week ago. The tech firm has become the latest business to delay its public listing, with experts saying the IPO market is getting more challenging. Oura's chief executive Tom Hale said "an IPO is just one step in our journey", adding that "we have the luxury of choosing our moment". Earlier this month, US nuclear technology firm Holtec International also postponed its flotation. It blamed an "unusual confluence of developments that has impaired investor confidence in the market for new public offerings". In particular, it cited rising energy costs, military conflicts, global trade tensions and concerns about inflation which have led to central banks including the US Federal Reserve raising benchmark interest rates. This week, the yield – or interest rate – on US debt repayable in 10 years' time hit the highest level since 2007. Samuel Kerr, global head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, said: "What is now clear is we are in a very different IPO market to the one we envisaged just a few weeks ago." Oura had planned to sell shares priced at between $40 and $44 on the Nasdaq stock market index, giving the company an implied market value of $15bn. In its last full financial year, ending 30 September 2025, Oura made a pre-tax profit of $23.5m on sales $907.8m. That compares to a $6.2m pre-tax profit in the previous year. Its most recent figures for the nine months to 30 June this year show pre-tax income of $70m on sales of $1.2bn. Oura, founded in Finland in 2013, has its global headquarters in San Francisco and makes smart rings – costing upwards of $300 – which monitor things such as its owner's heartbeat and sleep patterns which are analysed and presented on an app. The company is the subject of a class action lawsuit which accused it of false advertising by claiming its rings can accurately track a person's sleep activity and patterns. The lawsuit, filed by the Clarkson Law Firm in August, claimed: "Oura rings cannot measure one's sleep or cycles. That's because sleep happens in the brain, not on one's finger." It is understood that Oura's decision to delay an IPO is not connected to the lawsuit. In a statement, a spokesperson for Oura said: "We stand behind our science, research and accuracy claims." They added: "Like other consumer sleep wearables, Oura Ring estimates sleep stages using multiple physiological signals, including heart rate, heart rate variability, movement, breathing patterns, and temperature." events.title: OpenAI unveils its Muse competitor: Dots
events.summary: The News OpenAI on Tuesday launched a personalized agent tool, called dots — a new competitor to Meta’s popular Muse system. Dots “can do nearly anything,” OpenAI said, and integrates into applications like Slack and Microsoft Teams. People will soon be able to text with their dot, which can take action on a user’s behalf using a separate machine in the cloud. The launch shows OpenAI is betting it can turn its massive consumer advantage into a win on the agentic side. Meta got off to an early lead with Muse, which has been downloaded more than 3 million times. Like Muse, dots also features cutesy mascots that users can name, another indication that tech companies are banking on cuddly, personalized aesthetics to push the mass-market adoption of agents, which can access a much wider range of data than an ordinary chatbot and requires little technical know-how. But the agents’ expanded autonomy has come with friction: Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site; a Meta agent also recently gave out a Toronto man’s home address on Facebook Marketplace without his permission. Know More Earlier on Tuesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told CNBC he has tried Muse — it “seems like a nice product,” he said — but that he doesn’t feel threatened by Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg. Tech companies are promoting consumer-oriented and productivity-focused tools amid broader concerns over AI safety with its most powerful models. OpenAI said Monday it was delaying the release of its next-generation AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, citing internal testing that showed it didn’t meet safety standards. The company on Tuesday introduced an upgrade to its cheaper, mid-tier GPT-6 Sol model. A host of tech leaders also met at the White House on Tuesday to discuss AI and Washington’s strategy for the technology.

events.title: Solomon leaves Waldron with a clean slate
events.summary: Liz’s view Lloyd Blankfein, contemplating his exit from Goldman Sachs, liked to say that when things are bad, you can’t leave, and when things are good, you don’t want to. Blankfein was finally having fun, after a decade as CEO, when he started laying the groundwork for his exit in 2017. That’s where David Solomon will be in 2028, which The Wall Street Journal reports is the loose timeframe for him handing the reins to his longtime lieutenant, John Waldron. There’s little drama here: Waldron has followed a step behind Solomon since the 1990s, from Bear Stearns to Goldman and then up through its banking arm, and has had the heir apparent title to himself for Solomon’s entire run — something no incoming Goldman CEO in Goldman’s history can say. (He also turned down $500 million and a write-your-own-ticket offer from Apollo when it tried to scoop him up in 2024, not something one does without assurances.) Goldman has a history of chewing through CEOs-in-waiting. Neither John Thain nor John Thornton succeeded Hank Paulson. Gary Cohn tired of life as Prince Charles under Blankfein. Waldron will get the prize, and good timing, benefitting from Solomon’s stabilizing march but inheriting none of the baggage of his early tenure. Solomon had the Jack Welch-ian temperament to remake Goldman and, early on, the room to do it. He spent that capital on a disastrous foray into consumer banking — started before he became CEO but expanded on his watch — then spent his middle years putting down the resulting internal mutiny and mending fences with regulators. Goldman today looks like a more profitable, organized, and top-down version of its pre-2008 self. And its stock price, which is a decent proxy for the resting pulse inside 200 West Street, has quadrupled since he took the job. Unless he strikes the big deal that plenty of people, myself included, have long assumed he wants, Solomon will be remembered as a stabilizing, corporatizing leader of Wall Street’s premier institution. The transformation, if it comes, will be Waldron’s. The 56-year-old has staked out ground on AI and China , the two forces likely to define his tenure, and is a dealmaker at heart. Solomon leaves him with a clean slate. Notable Goldman Sachs’ stock price has more than quadrupled under Solomon since he took the reins back in October 2018.

events.title: Meet OpenAI's "dots" — a new AI assistant meant to take on Meta's Muse.
events.summary: OpenAI launched dots, its take on the AI assistant and an answer to Meta's Muse, a personal agent that has gone viral and moved markets since its release. Why it matters: ChatGPT defined the chatbot era, but that status will have to be earned again as the world shifts from talking with AI to making it go out and do things. What they're saying : "This is the real deal version of AI we've always imagined," Altman said of dots at the OpenAI developer event, adding that it is inspired by the "cool" examples of AI assistants we've all seen in movies for years. Driving the news: Dots, as OpenAI calls them, are agents that can be instructed to perform a wide range of tasks. Users provide a goal to a dot and set boundaries for what it can do on its own. The assistant can keep work moving in the background and reach out when it needs attention or more detail to complete a task. Dots "are an extension of you," OpenAI says, and are meant to compete with a growing crop of consumer-focused AI assistants that people have used to book travel, cancel subscriptions and for all manner of other tasks. The big picture: Agents are all the rage, and while the technology or goal is often the same, the approaches and capabilities vary, especially for Meta and OpenAI. Meta dove head first into the consumer market, launching Muse widely to its massive multi-billion-number user base, with the app topping the download charts in its early days of availability. OpenAI is targeting high-end subscribers, mostly developers, at least in the beginning. Apple's AI isn't really at the agent stage, but given its prominence on the iPhone, the newly revamped Siri will still be part of the conversation. Other start-ups, such as Instinct, are also taking aim at this space. OpenAI took the risk of live demos at the event, creating some oohs and ahas at times, but also saw a couple fails as well, such as when OpenAI's Holly Li tried to speak to her dot "dottie" and there was a lag. At the other end of the extreme, Apple has moved to entirely recorded videos for its product launches. Zoom in : Dots are available to Pro, Business and Enterprise users, with one dot per user to start. OpenAI says it eventually envisions teams of dots working together. Powered by GPT-6 Astra, each dot has its own cloud computer and can work across connected apps, Codex and ChatGPT Work to research, analyze data, prepare documents and build software. OpenAI also debuted GPT-6.1 Sol, which it says delivers near-Astra performance at one-fifth the cost. The company is lowering usage caps for new $200-a-month ChatGPT Pro customers. Existing customers will be able to keep their limits for an unspecified time. As OpenAI moves toward power users as a first-adopter assistant strategy, Muse is moving towards the workplace. Earlier Tuesday, Meta announced Muse now can connect to a range of tools used by small businesses.

events.title: ChatGPT's new plan costs $500 a month
events.summary: Sam Altman leads OpenAI. The company announced a new subscription tier, costing $500 a month. Selcuk Acar/Anadolu via Getty Images OpenAI announced a $500 a month plan for ChatGPT. The Pro 500 plan includes access to "Ultrafast" computing, offering an 8x speed increase in Codex. The company also downgraded the compute allowance of its $200 a month plan. ChatGPT has a brand new plan — with a hefty new price tag. OpenAI announced a new subscription tier at its Tuesday DevDay. The Pro 500 plan will cost $500 a month, a $300 increase on what was formerly the company's most expensive plan. The $500 plan will include access to "Ultrafast" computing for GPT-6 Astra in ChatGPT Work and Codex. The "Ultrafast" option promises an 8x increase in speed in Codex, OpenAI's coding tool . The tier will also have OpenAI's highest included usage. While the average ChatGPT user may not care about this, it's top of mind for any coder who has hit their token limit . Some eagle-eyed X users spotted test code for a $500 a month plan last week. $500 a month is steep, totaling out to $6,000 a year. And that's only for OpenAI; AI subscribers could also hold subscriptions with Anthropic or Cursor. Still, AI lovers previously told Business Insider that the highest-priced tier — then $200 a month — was worth it. Some considered it a necessary expense for their small businesses. events.title: Barclays softens return-to-office plans for UK staff after backlash
events.summary: Bank allows employees to delay being in workplace at least three days a week until 2027, if permission granted Barclays has watered down its return-to-office plans after a major staff backlash , with the bank allowing some employees to wait until next year before having to be in at least three days a week. The bank this summer announced the attendance requirement would come in for its 45,000 UK staff from 5 October, with more senior employees expected to come in for at least four days. That compares with current rules requiring staff to come in for two days. Now Barclays has offered a reprieve after thousands of bank staff signed an open letter drafted by the Unite union, calling for payouts to help cover travel costs and an exemption for those living more than 40 minutes from work. The bank will allow staff to delay complying with the order until 2027. However, they will need to ask and receive permission to do so from their line manager by the end of this week. In a memo emailed to staff, Barclays’ executive committee announced: “We are extending the implementation period for UK colleagues to ensure colleagues have the right support as we move through the transition … We are also reviewing our flexible working policy.” The extension, first reported by the Financial Times, could give unions more time to request further concessions. Barclays and Unite said they would continue discussions on the issue, which has become a flashpoint across the banking sector. Banks ranging from JP Morgan to Revolut have clamped down on remote working after the Covid pandemic, arguing it harms the training of younger staff. Unite have said that while they recognise face-to-face working can support collaboration, team development and relationship building: “We do not accept that this requires a blanket, one-size-fits-all increase in mandatory office attendance.” The union has requested a series of concessions, including: Automatic exemptions of in-office attendance rules during school holidays and Christmas. Capping in-office requirements at one day a week for any carers or people with disabilities. Flexible start and finish times to allow for cheaper off-peak travel costs and to accommodate school pickup and drop-offs. A single, consolidated payment made to all staff to make up for the costs of coming into the office, before March 2027. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning A spokesperson said: “Unite is continuing to engage with Barclays on its proposals relating to colleagues’ working arrangements.” In an emailed statement, a Barclays spokesperson said: “Our updated onsite working arrangements will take effect as planned. “We have continued to listen to colleague feedback to ensure colleagues have the right support while enabling us to deliver the benefits of working together in person. This includes transitional measures for those whose personal circumstances currently prevent them from meeting the new arrangements.”

events.title: Proteinmaxxing shows a ‘meaningful shift’ in how Gen Z takes supplements versus baby boomers, new survey shows
events.summary: Nowadays, you can find protein in pretty much every section of American grocery stores—beyond the typical meat aisle. Thirsty? Protein shakes and soda are on the shelves. Hungry? Aisle 20 has got all your meals covered with protein cereal, coffee, chips, and even mac n cheese.  With all that proteinmaxxing , younger Americans might seem like a generation that is obsessed with supplements, but new data complicates that picture. Adults under 30 are less likely than other age groups to take supplements for their health, according to a new Pew Research Center survey .  However, one supplement breaks that pattern: protein. Thirty-seven percent of adults ages 18 to 29 take protein supplements such as powders, drinks, or bars, compared to 23% of Americans 65 and older. This divide raises a bigger question about what taking a “supplement” looks like when protein is also showing up in everyday foods and drinks. Young Americans may not be abandoning wellness so much as changing how it fits into their everyday lives.  “We’re seeing a meaningful shift in how younger consumers engage with wellness and functional ingredients,” Scott Dicker, senior director of market insights at consumer data firm SPINS, told Fortune . While older generations have tended to prefer traditional supplement formats such as capsules, tablets, and powders, he said younger consumers are more likely to seek similar benefits through foods and beverages. “Rather than viewing supplements as a separate health regimen, younger consumers increasingly see function as something that can be incorporated into the products they’re already consuming throughout the day,” Dicker said. That can blur the line between a supplement and a snack. A multivitamin clearly looks like a supplement, while a protein shake or bar can also fit into a meal or an afternoon snack. And when it comes to a traditional vitamin cabinet—the age divide is especially stark. Just 48% of adults under 30 take vitamins or minerals, according to Pew, compared to 81% of those 65 and older. Overall supplement use follows a similar pattern: 67% of the youngest adults take at least one, compared with 85% of seniors. Protein reverses that pattern. A 2025 SPINS study of younger shoppers found that more than half of Gen Z and millennial shoppers surveyed said they follow a high-protein diet. But their interest in these “protein-fortified” foods doesn’t mean they’re giving up powders, drinks, or bars. Dicker said those core protein products are still performing well, even as companies add protein to products such as cereal, pasta, and soda. “You can’t walk in any aisle in the grocery store without seeing protein-enhanced products,” Dicker told Fortune .  The protein products different generations want also differ. Older consumers tend to favor foods naturally high in protein, such as yogurt and cottage cheese, while younger consumers gravitate toward products with added protein in categories that traditionally had little of it, such as cereal, Dicker said. Protein’s age paradox  But the age divide around protein consumption is somewhat counterintuitive from a nutritional standpoint. While the youngest adults are more likely to consume protein supplements, maintaining muscle becomes increasingly important as people get older. Roger Clemens, a professor at USC’s Mann School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences who has studied nutrition for decades, pointed to sarcopenia —the involuntary loss of muscle mass and strength that occurs with age—as one reason protein becomes an important consideration for older adults. “Protein is quite complicated,” Clemens told Fortune . He said the amount of a nutrient listed on a food or supplement label doesn’t tell consumers the full nutritional picture because how the body absorbs and uses it matters, too. The Pew findings alone can’t tell us whether the divide is truly generational or partly a product of age. Today’s 22-year-old protein-shake drinker could eventually become tomorrow’s multivitamin buyer as their health needs and routines change. Dicker said protein itself is no longer just for young people trying to build muscle—older consumers are also seeking it to help preserve muscle as they age. What is already changing is what companies put on shelves. Dicker said the shift is reshaping what supplement makers and food and beverage companies develop, as they increasingly build functional benefits into products consumers already buy. “For brands, this means meeting consumers where they are,” Dicker said. “Rather than asking consumers to adopt new supplement routines, many companies are embedding functional benefits into products that already fit seamlessly into everyday consumption occasions.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: What is the triple lock and why are people talking about it?
events.summary: The prime minister has announced plans to scrap the existing triple lock arrangement for the state pension in order to help fund a new plan for social care. The triple lock currently guarantees that the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% – whichever is the highest. Andy Burnham said he would honour the pledge given in Labour's 2024 manifesto to keep the triple lock unchanged in the current Parliament. However, the PM said that from April 2030 the arrangement will change, with the state pension rising every year at least by inflation or 2.5%. The link to rises in yearly average earnings, which is the factor currently setting the rise under the triple lock, will be gone on an annual basis and instead be reflected over time. What is the state pension and how much is it? The state pension is a payment made every four weeks by the government, to people who have reached the qualifying age and have paid enough National Insurance (NI) contributions. the new flat-rate state pension for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 is £241.30 a week, or £12,547.60 a year the old basic state pension for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 is £184.90 a week, or £9,614.80 a year Many people on the old basic state pension may also receive the additional state pension , external . In general, you need 35 years of qualifying contributions to get a full state pension. Some people may have gaps in their NI record if, for example, they have lived abroad or taken time off to care for children. It is possible to make voluntary payments to boost your contribution history. Since April 2025, you have only been able to make payments for the previous six years. Data suggested that the state pension will increase in April 2027 , meaning: the flat-rate state pension for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 will likely be £250.70 a week, or £13,036.40 a year, up £488 on now the old basic state pension for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 will likely be £192.10 a week, or £9,989.20 a year, up £374.40 on now The government will confirm the rise, possibly in October's Budget. Check your state pension forecast and whether you can increase it How does the state pension 'triple lock' work? Under the triple lock system, the state pension increases each April in line with whichever of three measures is the highest: inflation in the September of the previous year, using a measure called the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) the average increase in total wages, including bonuses, across the UK for May to July of the previous year The rise in wages of 3.9% is likely to determine the April 2027 state pension increase. The triple lock was introduced by the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government in 2010. It was designed to ensure the value of the state pension wasn't overtaken by the increase in the cost of living or the incomes of working people. The Labour government has previously said it would keep the triple lock until the end of the current Parliament. But since that commitment, there has been intense debate over the cost of the triple lock and whether it is justified. In July 2025, the government's official forecaster said the cost of the triple lock guarantee was set to be three times higher by the end of the decade than was originally anticipated when it began. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said the annual cost is set to reach £15.5bn by 2030. It said the cost of the state pension has risen steadily over the past eight decades, and now equates to £138bn, or around half the total amount the government spent on benefits. In July, the influential Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) think-tank suggested that the triple lock should be scrapped as part of a wider pensions overhaul. What has Andy Burnham said about the future of the triple lock? At his speech to the Labour Party conference, Burnham announced a plan to end the existing triple lock from 2030, which would see the annual link to earnings growth removed. "The state pension will continue to rise every year at least by prices or 2.5%," he said. "And it will hold its value relative to earnings over time so that pensioners will always share in the rising prosperity of the nation. "But this change will generate significant savings which we will use to build up our national care service." The IFS called the proposed change a "great improvement", saying Burnham had "neutered the worst element of the triple lock". "State pensions will still rise, but more sustainably," said Jonathan Cribb, deputy director at the IFS. However, he warned that "we should not expect this reform to save enough that it could fund universal social care in the next parliament". Will state pensioners pay income tax? The expected increase in April 2027 would take the flat-rate state pension above the personal allowance of £12,570 and so liable to pay about £91 next year in income tax.

events.title: My son has had screen time since he was 3 months old. I see it as a necessity for parenting.
events.summary: The author said screens are sometimes a necessity in a parent's life. (author's child not shown) Paulo Sousa/Getty Images I use screen time as a tool to balance parenting and my personal productivity needs. My son, 2, often watches educational content, Disney movies, and musicals. Watching TV helped my son develop social skills, and I have no regrets. It's a cloudy afternoon and my 2-year-old is watching "The Lego Movie," while my husband works his 9-to-5 job. I am in charge of our kid, the primary caregiver or stay-at-home-mom, if you will. But I have things to do too, and I can't afford a nanny. So for the next two hours, a movie will act as my babysitter. My kid is still and calm, safe on the couch while I type right next to him, checking things off my own to-do list. I'll be the first to admit it's not a perfect set-up, but it's a necessary one. The author said that her son has had screen time since he was a baby and she has noticed benefits from his time in front of the TV. Courtesy of Rachel Meghan. Screens were a necessity My child probably first laid eyes on a screen when he was 3 months old, and it's not something I regret. Many experts recommend that children not be exposed to screens until they are older than that. However, the only people I know among my mom friends who subscribe to this philosophy religiously are parents who can afford nannies, daily activities, or daycare. Do you have a hot take on a common parenting belief? Email Jennifer Beck Goldblatt at jgoldblatt@insider.com to share your experience with Business Insider. For some parents who stay at home, especially with younger children, they are likely doing so due to the cost of childcare outweighing the paycheck they'd be making at a job. So when are those parents, parents like me, supposed to get a break? There are benefits to screen time I believe that educational content can be very enriching for children, so I allow my son to watch " Ms. Rachel ," along with old '90s PBS shows like "Barney," which he watches on YouTube. These shows not only teach him skills that will prepare him for kindergarten but also teach empathy, kindness, and friendship. My son almost never throws tantrums, and I think a big part of that is the self-regulation he's learned from watching TV. For movies, he enjoys Disney movies and musicals. With the right curation from me, I see TV and film as a useful supplement for my child's growing brain. I also appreciate how it exposes him to culture. Films were a big part of my childhood memories, and I wouldn't want to deny my child the opportunity to grow up with old musicals and Disney movies, just like I did. Not all screens are equal in my mind I say all of this about screens with a big caveat: I don't think babies, toddlers, or even young children should have access to iPads . I have one that I use for work, but I've purposely kept it out of my toddler's hands. I don't think being so close to a screen and having unfiltered access to whatever the internet has to offer is good for a growing mind. I also closely monitor the content my child watches and will continue to do so as he grows. We avoid offerings that I find overstimulating. Screens are only part of our day Our son is not sitting in front of the TV all day. It's usually an hour or so, here and there. The author said her child does plenty outside of the house too, often visiting parks, museums, and the library. Courtesy of Rachel Meghan. We also take trips to the the park and local museums multiple times a week. I read to him every day, and we spend a lot of time at our library. Ours has many programs that encourage kids to read, and we have followed them religiously since he was big enough to visit, such as the summer reading program. This program awards prizes for every hour a child reads, and we complete it every year. In a perfect world, parents would have endless energy to entertain their children, and kids could be left to their own devices without fear of them getting themselves into trouble. But that's just not feasible for most stay-at-home parents. I know it's OK to take a break from time to time and put on a beloved movie for my kid to relax to. He's a person, too, and he deserves a break from the chaos as much as I do. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods TV & Home Entertainment Accessories Support Final Cut Camera now supports variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and even more pro options with iOS 27 iPhone 18 Pro shows a Final Cut Camera screen with settings for aperture, shutter, and ISO. iPhone 18 Pro shows a Final Cut Camera screen with a recording in progress and the new tally light. Text of this article September 29, 2026 UPDATE Final Cut Camera now supports variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and even more pro options with iOS 27 Final Cut Camera, the professional filming app for iPhone, receives a major update with version 2.4, adopting a new design, adding support for variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro, and giving creators even more pro options with the release of iOS 27. The new version is available as a free software update beginning today, September 29. Redesigned from the ground up, Final Cut Camera gives creators even easier access to popular settings like shutter angle, ISO, and white balance, along with customizable overlays, including false color and clipping indicators for proper exposure, and improved focus peaking with sensitivity control. A new tally light indicates when recording is underway, and a two-finger tap now clears the viewfinder so users can focus on the shot. With iPhone 18 Pro, users can take advantage of the new Fusion Main camera with variable aperture — the most advanced camera Apple has ever made — which brings aperture control to iPhone for the first time. Final Cut Camera allows creators to precisely dial in their aperture settings, or choose between shutter priority and aperture priority modes, to record stunning videos. The update also unlocks Cinematic mode effects for regular video, including footage captured in ProRes and Apple Log, allowing creators to adjust focus points and depth of field while editing in Final Cut Pro. With iOS 27, Final Cut Camera adds support for professional video scopes, clean SDI out, and genlock offset. Now creators can accurately monitor their video using the RGB Parade — which displays the red, green, and blue color channels to help check color balance and exposure — and the histogram. With clean SDI out, creators can send a clean video signal using an HDMI-to-SDI converter for broadcast-quality streaming. And with genlock offset, creators can compensate for image artifacts from a recorded display or for latency differences between their iPhone and other genlocked cameras. The plan is to launch an uncrewed vehicle, the Starliner-1, in the December 2026 / January 2027 timeframe, and a crewed vehicle, Starliner-2, sometime in 2028. Starliner-1 will ferry cargo to the International Space Station (ISS) and, if all goes well, humans will take their turn on Starliner-2. NASA also intends to exercise options for a fifth and sixth flight to and from the ISS and to get the Vulcan rocket certified for use after the Atlas V, which has launched Starliner to date, is finally phased out. In 2025, NASA pared back the Starliner contract and modified its order from six to four missions. At the time, Boeing was aiming for no earlier than April 2026 for Starliner-1, something that has now slipped to the end of the year and might go beyond. An observer might wonder what the point is of splashing cash on a program that has managed one crewed flight since the contract was awarded in 2014. 2024's flight test ended with an empty capsule returning to Earth after controllers decided multiple failures had made it too risky for humans. The crew, Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams, had to wait on the ISS for months until returning as part of the SpaceX Crew-9 mission . Boeing's Starliner has struggled, but SpaceX's Crew Dragon is proven and essential for getting crews to and from the ISS. Its run may be ending though. NASA recently added three more Crew Dragon missions to the ISS, and 2028 appears to be the end of the road (at least for now). That uncertainty, plus the coming wave of commercial stations that will need crew access, could give Starliner an opening. NASA says maintaining a US crew transportation capability is essential to winding down the ISS responsibly, transitioning to commercial stations, and expanding commercial success. Boeing stated that 19 of the 21 in-flight "anomalies" noted during the crew flight test are now closed, with the remainder due to close in October. Changes made to the spacecraft include the replacement of valves on all 12 of the crew module reaction control thrusters, improvements to the parachute joint design, and upgraded battery systems from NASA. It remains difficult to escape the words "sunk-cost fallacy" when considering the billions spent on the Starliner program. events.summary: Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods TV & Home Entertainment Accessories Support Apple and the American Academy of Pediatrics release new guide to help families build healthy digital habits Start a conversation about screen time , with tips for parents to approach the topic and establish expectations in a way that helps kids feel included in the plan. Make a schedule for device use , using Time Allowances and Schedules to balance time online with sleep, schoolwork, physical activity, and time with family and friends. Text of this article September 29, 2026 UPDATE Apple and the American Academy of Pediatrics release new guide to help families build healthy digital habits Today, in partnership with the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), Apple released a new guide to help families create healthy digital habits that balance screen time with sleep, exercise, schoolwork, and time with friends and family. The AAP’s expert guidance has been tailored for Apple’s new parental controls in “Building Healthy Digital Habits: A Guide for Families.” “Every family approaches technology in their own way,” said Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness. “That’s why we wanted to combine trusted guidance from the American Academy of Pediatrics with the tools built into our products. Together, they’re designed to adapt to each family and each child’s stage of development, giving parents a useful starting point to decide what works best. Our hope is that this guide helps facilitate easier discussions and gives families the resources they need to put this guidance into practice, adjust their approach as their child grows, and help them develop healthy digital habits they can carry into everyday life.” This guide walks families through six steps: Start a conversation about screen time , with tips for parents to approach the topic and establish expectations in a way that helps kids feel included in the plan. Create a Child Account , which enables age-based safeguards and gives parents access to parental controls to manage their child’s experience. Set safety settings for websites and apps , including Ask to Buy and Ask to Browse, so families can review new apps and websites together. Make a schedule for device use , using Time Allowances and Schedules to balance time online with sleep, schoolwork, physical activity, and time with family and friends. Manage communications , with parents deciding who their child can communicate with and Communication Safety, on by default for all users under 18, helping protect kids from viewing or sharing sensitive content. Continue the conversation as kids grow , with guidance on adjusting the family’s plan over time. There’s also more detailed information on the AAP’s screen time guidance by age group, from infants to teens, to help families consider their choices around media use. “At AAP, our focus is equipping pediatricians and families with trusted science-based guidance to support informed decisions at every stage of a child’s life, including building healthy digital habits,” said Mark Del Monte, the AAP’s chief executive officer. “We are proud to partner with Apple to expand access to the Family Media Plan, helping parents create routines that promote balance, safety, and healthy development. We know that navigating screens and social media is something every parent wants to get right, and this partnership will further support families with those efforts.” Learn more about Apple’s approach to child safety . Availability New features are available now with the Screen Time update in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27. All products in a Family Sharing group must be updated to iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 to use the Screen Time update. Some features may not be available in all regions, in all languages, or on all models. For more information about availability, visit apple.com . events.title: I attended pastry school in France. Here are 6 tips for making the best brownies.
events.summary: After attending pastry school and working in several bakeries, I've picked up a few tips for making the best brownies. Vrinda Mahesh/Getty Images After attending pastry school in France, I've learned the secrets to making the tastiest brownies. I've found using high-quality chocolate and thoroughly whipping the eggs leads to the best results. To elevate brownies even more, I like adding some nuts or caramel to the batter. I'm a full-time baker who has attended pastry school in France, completed a baking course in China, and worked in several bakeries in New York City. After spending countless hours in the kitchen testing numerous recipes over the years, I've learned what makes a delicious brownie, and what doesn't. Brownies may look simple and have a short ingredient list, but achieving that perfect chocolatey flavor and fudgy texture comes down to a few small details. Here are six tips for making perfect brownies at home. For the best flavor, I love using high-quality chocolate or cocoa powder. Roberto Machado Noa/Getty Images Since brownies are all about their rich flavor, I like to use a high-quality chocolate or cocoa powder . Because chocolate has varying levels of fruitiness and bitterness, it can drastically change the flavor of any dessert, so I always recommend experimenting with different flavor profiles to find what tastes best. For a darker color and richer flavor, I prefer Dutch-process cocoa powder over the regular version, which has a more reddish hue and can have acidic notes. Adding the cocoa powder to the melted butter prevents a clumpy batter. LumiNola/Getty Images To get the fudgiest brownies, I love adding the cocoa powder to melted butter, which helps break up any clumps that could remain in the final product. Once the butter is melted and still hot, I add the cocoa powder to the bowl and mix until smooth, then add the recipe's remaining ingredients. This process, called blooming, ensures the brownies have maximum flavor. Throwing some espresso into the batter adds so much flavor. Allison Chen To enhance the chocolate flavor in a brownie, I love to add 1 teaspoon of espresso powder or instant coffee to the batter. Coffee and chocolate share similar flavor characteristics that complement each other in baked goods, creating a deeper flavor. When combined in brownie batter, the bitterness of the espresso helps balance the chocolate's sweetness. Thoroughly beating the eggs creates a glossy finish. Allison Chen A well-made brownie is known for the shiny skin that forms on top in the oven. To achieve this, I always thoroughly whip the eggs with the sugar until they're light and fluffy and turn a pale yellow. This process, which can take up to 10 minutes, ensures that a large portion of the sugar dissolves into the eggs, helping to create a cracked top. Even though this step requires a bit of patience, it always leads me to the best results. Sprinkling in some unique toppings immediately elevates a brownie. Anne DEL SOCORRO/Getty Images Brownies are fantastic on their own, but they're also easy to customize with all sorts of toppings. I love folding in some chopped chocolate, nuts, or crushed cookies. Or, to really take it to the next level, I like swirling in peanut butter, tahini, or caramel — and finish with some flaky salt on top when they're right out of the oven. However, I never overload the batter with too many additions, since that could impact the texture and baking time. Likewise, a brownie can serve as a great base for whipped cream, vanilla ice cream , fruit, or a layer of chocolate ganache. My personal favorite is a brownie topped with tangy cream-cheese frosting. I never overbake the brownies. Grace Cary/Getty Images Brownie batter has a high sugar content, and too much time in the oven can result in very dry, chewy brownies due to excessive caramelization and a lack of moisture. So, I usually err on the side of underbaking the brownies rather than overdoing them. To test if the brownies are done, I just stick a toothpick in the center of the pan. The toothpick should have moist crumbs on it, since a completely cooked brownie may still be a little soft in the middle when fresh out of the oven. For clean slices, I let the brownies cool completely before cutting into them. To speed up this process, I sometimes chill them in the fridge for an hour. events.title: New AI-powered government website uses Gemini, Grok, Trump official Gebbia says
events.summary: The new Trump administration chatbot America.gov is powered by artificial intelligence from Google's Gemini and Elon Musk's Grok, U.S. Chief Design Officer Joe Gebbia said. The new site is being unveiled at a day-long event attended by President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance and other administration officials and industry leaders. The Trump administration's new chatbot aimed at helping Americans navigate official government websites is powered by artificial intelligence from Google 's Gemini and Elon Musk 's Grok, U.S. Chief Design Officer Joe Gebbia said Tuesday. "We have great partners behind the scenes," Gebbia told CNBC's " Squawk Box " shortly before the site, America.gov , went live around 10 a.m. ET. A Google spokesperson referred CNBC to a company blog post published Tuesday morning, which said, "Google is proud to be named a technology partner in this vital initiative, leveraging Gemini to help more than 100 million people access critical public resources with greater speed and ease." "By supporting the administration's vision for digital modernization, we are committed to making these everyday public services seamless, accessible, and responsive for all Americans," the post read. Grok developer xAI, which was acquired by SpaceX and renamed SpaceXAI, did not respond to CNBC's request for comment. Gebbia sits on the board of directors of Tesla, which is led by Musk, owns a piece of SpaceXAI and uses Grok in its vehicles. "Every day, 40 million people interact with a government website trying to get something done. And I think we could all agree that we wish it was better," Gebbia told CNBC. Trump holds up to $1 billion in bonds tied to institutions he can affect Rep. James Comer expands House investigation into prediction market insider trading Hassett: 'We're still working our way out from' Biden Covid spending The AI tool interacts with all of the roughly 29,000 government websites to respond to user questions with up-to-date information, Gebbia said. "You come to America.gov and you ask for what you need, and in a chat interface, we go off on the back end and scan across all those tens of thousands of websites to pull in any information that is specific to whatever your request is, and give you a personalized response that's only from official sources," he said. "So there's no chance of getting outdated or inaccurate information like you might on third-party websites." The site is being unveiled at a day-long event in Washington's Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium, attended by President Donald Trump , Vice President JD Vance and other administration officials and industry leaders. "It's not just simply a website. It's a restoration of America's founding promise, and it's a reinvention of your government for the 21st century and beyond," Trump said in a speech at the event. The gathering will also include a range of panel discussions on AI and other topics, including, energy, health, space and agriculture. — CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.

events.title: Faisal Islam: Triple lock move is significant, but it's a gamble
events.summary: It was a significant announcement from Prime Minister Andy Burnham on his plans for the triple lock after the general election. It will reverberate well beyond the hall. For months, I have heard suggestions that Andy Burnham was warm to the idea that the triple lock as we know it had to go. I had expected him to try to forge a political consensus on this thorny issue at this stage, but he has gone further than that. He has tried to take the sting out of the politics of his decision by tying it to funding a new national social care service. The government calls it an "adjusted triple lock" as it is keen that pensioners are reassured. It is more like a double lock plus. The sensitivity over this political gamble is clear. Under Burnham's plans, the state pension will go up by either the pace of price rises or 2.5%, whichever is higher. So, it will still keep up with inflation and go up every year. The link to rises in yearly average earnings, which is the factor currently setting the rise under the triple lock, will be gone on an annual basis and instead be reflected over time. The policy would be to maintain the state pension as a share of earnings at the record level it is due to reach in 2030. This change is sharper than expected. Not a review or a consultation. Ministers and MPs will have to back the plans in interviews and, at some point, MPs will have to vote on changing the historic annual earnings link to the state pension. It seems far more significant than a mere "adjustment". This will save many billions in the coming decades, but not so much in the next few years. The Institute for Fiscal Studies thinktank says that, had Burnham's tweak been in place since 2011, it would have more than halved the annual £16bn cost of the triple lock, a £9bn saving every year. Government sources said the decision to make the change now will save around £15bn a year by 2040. The prime minister was repeatedly advised that bond markets would show some appreciation for a UK government capable of taking tough decisions. Former chancellor Rachel Reeves might have imagined the same reward for her decision to scrap the winter fuel allowance, which was one of her first acts and later reversed. Part of the UK premium in bond markets has been an understandable perception that UK politics cannot have long-term debates. And the triple lock is only one of the debates started by today's speech – with significant further moves on energy and post-Brexit policy expected – that the prime minister and chancellor need the markets as well as the country to get behind. What are your views on the triple lock? Watch: How did Burnham's speech go down in the conference hall? events.title: The FBI is looking into a new possible ransom note connected to the disappearance of Nancy Guthrie
events.summary: Authorities are looking into the possibility of a new ransom note related to the disappearance of Nancy Guthrie , nearly eight months after she went missing from her Arizona home, the Pima County Sheriff’s Department said. The sheriff’s department and the FBI Guthrie Task Force were recently made aware of the possible ransom note as well as social media comments related to it, the statement from the sheriff’s department said Monday. Investigators are working to determine its credibility. Officials did not immediately release details on how they found the note or what was in it. In July, authorities released two ransom notes initially sent to a Tucson television station days after the mother of “Today” show host Savannah Guthrie went missing on Feb. 1 from her home outside Tucson. The first note, sent Feb. 2 , said Nancy Guthrie was safe but scared and would be released unharmed once her captors received $4 million in cryptocurrency. The second note, sent Feb. 6, said Guthrie died shortly after she was kidnapped. Authorities have not said whether Guthrie is still alive. No suspects have been arrested in her disappearance. The investigation is dogged by unanswered questions, such as how many people are believed to have taken part in her abduction and whether she was taken by someone who knew her. The FBI had also released surveillance videos of a masked person who authorities said appeared to tamper with a camera on Nancy Guthrie’s front porch and block it with a plant. Nancy Guthrie’s family has shared their pleas for information in videos posted to social media. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Conference laps up Andy unplugged as he offers chance to take road less travelled | John Crace
events.summary: Conference laps up Andy unplugged as he offers chance to take road less travelled Nothing was off the table, no coded hints, and by the end no one could be in any doubt about what Burnham believed Y ou’ve got to hand it to Andy Burnham. He left nothing out on the pitch. It would have been so easy to play it safe. To deliver a traditional leader’s speech to a home crowd. One we’ve been seeing from leaders of all parties for more than 15 years. Something warm, a feelgood vibes word salad with the odd minor spending announcement thrown in. Hell, the Labour conference would have probably settled for it. They already had all the hope that they had come for . The hope that they were back in with a fighting chance of winning the next election. They wouldn’t have even dared think that three months ago. But Andy did it differently . Just as he had promised. He had said he was a different kind of politician and he duly made good on that. Hope came with honesty, he said. And honesty was what we got. Nothing was redacted. No coded hints. Come the end of his hour-long speech, no one could be in any doubt about what he thought. More than that, what he believed. Not so much a speech, more an article of faith. This was Andy unplugged. Unmediated. That most elusive of hybrids. The career politician who can still make the political personal and deliver it fearlessly. Keir Starmer could never have done this, even if he had wanted to. He was just too naturally cautious. A man one step removed from himself. Andy was running on pure emotion. Some things you can’t fake. At one point, just as he was about to talk about his dad, he choked up. Unable to speak. It became a moment of communion. Burnham was not going to die wondering. He knew he might be delivering one of the longest suicide notes in history, but he did it anyway. Because he couldn’t not do it. Better to go down remaining true to his principles than being slowly airbrushed out of history like the previous six prime ministers. Failures all. Andy was prepared to burn through all his political capital right there in Liverpool, right then. Not just for his own legacy but for a country he wanted to rebuild. It was the only way he could look himself in the mirror. Honour his parents. It goes without saying that Andy was received with a long series of near rapturous standing ovations throughout the speech. The audience was only too happy to be a pushover. Even the physicist Brian Cox. He was up and down like a yo-yo. If there were any black holes in the sums, he was far too polite to point them out. Not that this was a speech where anything so grubby as actual numbers were spelled out. This was all big-picture stuff. A reimagined vision of the future. Where the country didn’t feel permanently broke and broken. “All together now,” Burnham began. That would be his rallying cry. And he put his money where his mouth was. So many politicians use their conference speeches to trash the other parties. Many of the cabinet have done just that this week. But Andy didn’t once namecheck his rivals or use them to score points. The closest he got was to say we would all have failed if we voted in a divisive party on a vote of less than 30%. He would rather work with opposition parties for the common good. Fat chance. This is never going to happen. The idea of getting Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch round a table and agreeing to a unified sense of purpose was never going to happen. Kemi is unable to even agree with herself. But it sounded good. On message with brand Burnham. And Andy is no fool. That’s why most of the changes were ones that would be up for grabs at the next election. He wasn’t about to rat out on the manifesto that Labour had campaigned and won on. That would be a breach of trust. Not the Burnham way. This was a line in the sand. A chance for the country to take the road less travelled. It was up to voters whether they wanted to follow Burnham or stick with a decade of failure. That included Keir. Andy did give his predecessor a passing nod of thanks for winning the election but his heart wasn’t really in it. Later in the speech, he talked of the key moments in Labour history. 1945. 1964. 1997. And now. Not 2024. Keir was a has-been. A leader in the school of failure. Nothing was off the table. Social care. Bring it on. Other politicians of all parties had been content to ignore it on the grounds that it was just too difficult to sort out. Far better that old people should die of dementia in their own piss and shit than politicians be forced to make decisions that might cost them a general election. Just keep calm, tinker around the edges and carry on. The triple lock. For years, most economists have been saying the triple lock is financially unsustainable and has redressed the imbalance in pensions for which it was introduced. But no party had dared touch it. Terrified that old people would take their revenge at the ballot box.

events.title: We moved to a small island with our 10-month-old after finding a house for $1,000 a month that felt too good to be true
events.summary: We moved to a small island in Maine, and have found it to be a great place to raise kids. Jenna Mann When looking for a three-bedroom home , we found a place for $1,000 on an island in Maine. We took a trip with our baby, fell in love with the island, and decided to move there. Three years later, I'm so glad we moved here, despite the occasional challenges. Three years ago, we were in Indiana. My husband Kevin was finishing grad school , and I was absently, fruitlessly scrolling through Zillow while our baby was napping in his crib. Kevin had just secured a remote job, which opened the whole country up to us. This was exciting, until I realized we needed three bedrooms: one for us, one for our baby, and a third for a remote workspace . A three-bedroom house on one income is hard to swing in most parts of the country, and I was feeling increasingly depressed about my search. We're both from New Jersey, and we really wanted to get back to the coast. It quickly became apparent that homes in New Jersey were out of our price range, so I kept zooming out (and out and out) on the map, certain that we'd have nowhere to go. And that's when a little pin popped up off the coast of Maine. At first, the opportunity seemed too good to be true I clicked on the listing and saw a three-bedroom house priced at $1,000 a month. After all of my searching, this really felt unlikely. Even more suspicious: The only picture was a blueprint. The house hadn't even been built yet. Some more sleuthing revealed that the project was being led by the Cranberry Isles Realty Trust (CIRT), an organization that provides affordable year-round housing on both Great and Little Cranberry Island. The website described a tight-knit community set against a backdrop of ocean, pine trees, boats docked in a harbor, and the mountains of Acadia National Park across the bay. At this point in my life, I hadn't even considered there being towns on islands that were only accessible by boat. Once we confirmed the listing was indeed real, we had some questions … and some big conversations. Deciding where to go is hard on its own, but choosing where to move with a young baby is even tougher. We weren't just deciding where to live, but where our baby would first learn about the world. The idea that he could experience untouched nature right outside our door was enticing. As was the idea of raising him in a real community, one where everyone knows each other and where the older kids roam free together in the summer — something that I didn't think existed anymore. The deal also felt too good to pass up. It didn't feel like we could comfortably live anywhere else in the country for $1,000 a month. This opportunity was strange, new, and a little scary, but also exciting … so we put in our application. We fell in love with the island immediately We fell in love with Great Cranberry Island the first time we visited. Jenna Mann At first, it was just a daydream. We weren't sure we'd get selected — and weren't even sure we would move if we were — but it was a nice life to imagine. About a month later, we got an email that we were scheduled for an interview, and we decided it was time to take a trip out to the island. We took a road trip with our then-4-month-old, and the next morning, we got on a small boat. This boat is the official mail boat for the islands, meaning it transports all of our packages. It also transports people — this is how those without their own boats travel back and forth to the mainland. We left our car behind and took the 20-minute commute to the place we would eventually call home. It was a less-than-ideal June day, 56 degrees and raining. And still, the peace we felt in that moment is what lingered in our minds for months as we considered the potential of this move. What struck us most was the quiet. There were no highways, and not a lot of people. We learned that there are around 60 year-round residents, and 250 in the summer. Surprisingly, it was soothing to realize that without a boat, we wouldn't be able to go anywhere until the ferry came back: When you're here, you're here. It was a sense of place and presence I hadn't experienced anywhere else. For two people from New Jersey , where there are a million places to go at all times, this was thrilling. And it set still an anxiety I have had running inside me for decades. There are challenges, but I'm so glad we moved here I've loved raising my two young sons here. Jenna Mann Of course, living on Great Cranberry Island also comes with difficulties. A trip to the grocery store or a doctor's appointment can end up taking the whole day. The ferry schedule determines when we have to rush back to the boat. Sometimes there are several days in a row when the boats don't run because of the wind, so we have to keep too many diapers on hand at all times, and reusable ones on standby. The winters here are long, too, and the feeling of isolation starts to creep up on you. All of this is outweighed, though, by the breathtaking beauty of this place and a community that scrambles to help one another when needed. I question almost everything I do as a parent, but when my boys (now plural, ages two and three) confidently navigate the trails, or hand me sea glass on the beach, or greet our island neighbors by name and with a smile, I'm certain we're in the right place — and I feel so lucky to have found it. Then you won't be keen on the latest Word bug Redmond to millions of Power BI users: You’re Fabric app devs now 9 hours ago What eldritch horror lurks behind Heathrow's information screens? 10 hours ago JadePuffer crims hijacked Azure identities and used them to blow up cloud resources 23 hours ago Microsoft's Copilot super app comes with a meter attached 1 day ago Dutch government turns to NixOS for a sovereign desktop 1 day ago Microsoft has confirmed a bug where saving a PDF from Word for Windows can send the file to an unexpected location with a random name when using SharePoint Online. The Windows giant's odyssey of bork has continued, following issues that included a less-than-ideal September for its flagship operating system and a paste problem in Excel . The latest breakage affects the document format PDF in Word for Windows. After a user updates to version 2609 of Word, saving documents as PDFs to SharePoint Online locations can produce a nasty surprise. For starters, the file is saved in C:\Users\[username]\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\INetCache\Content.MSO instead, with a random filename. Worse, Word shows no error to indicate anything went wrong. According to Microsoft, "The issue only occurs when using Save/Save As, choosing the PDF file type, and selecting a SharePoint location." Use the Export option, or save somewhere else, and all will be well. The Register asked Microsoft if it is working on a fix and when one might be incoming, but the company has yet to respond. Some affected users have reported that rolling back the update resolves the issue. Microsoft's customers have had a torrid time of it lately. As well as the paste glitch, a seemingly innocuous Microsoft 365 update inadvertently deactivated Office 2016 and 2019 , and the company recently admitted it had accidentally wiped out some customers' Microsoft 365 data before the expiry of their retention period. Then there is the ongoing saga of the September Windows update, which caused bugs so severe that Microsoft rushed out an out-of-band update. That out-of-band update brought troubles of its own: on top of lingering audio problems and issues with domain-joined devices, Microsoft admitted that customers using File History might be unable to create or update backups. events.title: Man City guilty of all serious financial breach charges: Premier League
events.summary: Manchester City say they are ‘disappointed and surprised’ by the verdict and will appeal. Manchester City have been found guilty of ⁠all charges ⁠of serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, the league has said in ⁠a statement. City were charged in February 2023 with breaches of the league’s financial rules spanning the nine seasons following ⁠a four-year investigation. The club said in a statement it would appeal. An independent commission found that City “arranged ‘sham’ contracts” with a number of its commercial partners that misrepresented the true agreement between the parties, the league said on Tuesday. The league added that the commission had found City used schemes “to artificially inflate the club’s revenues, and reduce its costs, by more than 900 million pounds ($1.2bn) during the affected period, to appear to comply with financial rules”. “The ⁠core decision … details how the club systematically ⁠broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade,” said Richard Masters, chief executive of the Premier League. “There are elements of the case that remain to be ⁠decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches,” he said. City, who deny any wrongdoing, said ⁠they were “disappointed and surprised” by the ⁠commission’s opinion. “The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its ‌positions, relating to this case,” the club said. “Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the ‌basis ‌that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.” The commission found City arranged commercial deals whereby companies were only required to pay a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees. The remainder was funded by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment and Development, which owned the club. Further arrangements, funded by the group, enabled the club to record lower operating expenses than they actually incurred. The commission found they would have breached spending limits “by a very substantial amount” if City had reported accurately. In addition, the club were found to have “made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League” during the investigation. “It’s incredibly serious, the Premier League report is incredibly stark,” said the United Kingdom government’s Culture, Media and Sport Secretary Lisa Nandy. Since a 2008 takeover from Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates, City have become the Premier League’s dominant force. They have won eight Premier League titles, four FA Cups and seven League Cups over the past 15 years and also won the Champions League for the first time in 2023. But that same year they were charged by the Premier League on more than 100 charges following an investigation into alleged breaches of rules. According to Premier League rules, the sanction can vary from a points deduction, a fine or even expulsion from the division. Everton and Nottingham Forest were handed points deductions in the 2023-24 season for single breaches of financial sustainability rules. On that basis, City would face likely relegation if the same penalty is applied for over 100 charges. David Bernstein , who served as City chairman from 1998 to 2003, said the club should be expelled from the Premier League after the guilty verdict. “It is damning beyond belief. My immediate thoughts are, should the board continue? Should the people involved be suspended immediately?” Bernstein told the BBC. “Very, very serious. I think it’s really terrible. There’s a school of thought with lawyers that is deny, deny, deny, but this is a football club that is part of a league and the whole credibility of the league is at stake here. “The sanctions cannot just be financial, so it’s got to be way beyond that. If the appeal fails, Manchester City cannot stay in the league, they have to suffer. And I say that as a supporter and a fan.”
